blocks.text: American footwear brand Converse has pulled an advert that social media users said evoked Ku Klux Klan imagery, saying it recognised "that we got this wrong".
The photo, posted to the company's Instagram account, received backlash online after critics described lighting in the image as looking like a white pointed hood.
A pair of shoes, dangling in the picture, were also likened to an image of a lynching victim by social media users.

In an apology, first issued on Friday, Converse said the photo had been removed from its social media channels and it was working to remove it elsewhere. "This should not have happened and we will do better," it said.
The statement also said: "We're sorry. We understand why this image is deeply upsetting and recognize that we got this wrong".

articles.title: P12/L fuel subsidy on hold amid BSKE ban on social services spending
articles.summary: The Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB) has suspended the distribution of the P12-per-liter fuel subsidy for public utility vehicle (PUV) drivers due to the election ban on…

blocks.text: Published September 19, 2026 10:03pm

The Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB) has suspended the distribution of the P12-per-liter fuel subsidy for public utility vehicle (PUV) drivers due to the election ban on public spending for social services ahead of the upcoming Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections (BSKE).

In a "24 Oras Weekend" report by Bernadette Reyes on Saturday, several jeepney drivers expressed frustration over the suspension, appealing to the government to either increase the fuel subsidy or approve their pending request for a fare hike.

“’Yung ibinigay nilang subsidy, dagdagan nila kasi ayaw nilang taasan ‘yung pamasahe eh tapos taas nang taas ’yung [presyo ng] diesel. Paano naman kaming mga drayber?” said Arturo Vinluan, a jeepney driver.
(They should increase the subsidy if they refuse to raise fares, especially with diesel prices continuously rising. What will happen to us drivers?)
Another driver said he might temporarily stop plying his route because of low passenger volume and soaring fuel costs.
“Gagarahe na muna kasi walang pasahero, walang sakay, hangga’t wala pa 'yung subsidy namin. Sobrang taas eh. Wala naman gaanong sakay,” the driver said.
(I’m just going to park the vehicle for now while waiting for our subsidy. Fuel prices are just too high, and there aren’t many passengers.)
Under the election code, public welfare and social service programs are prohibited during the election period unless granted an exemption by the Commission on Elections (Comelec).
The Comelec said it is open to allowing the fuel subsidy to proceed once an exemption is requested. However, it has yet to receive a formal request from the LTFRB.
Trip adjustments
At a bus terminal in Sampaloc, Manila, a bus company was forced to cut trips and adjust departure schedules to cope with rising fuel prices.
In Reyes' report, a bus bound for Tuguegarao that was originally scheduled to depart at 8 a.m. remained at the terminal past 9 a.m. because only four passengers had boarded.
The bus operator explained that it needs a higher passenger turnout to avoid operating at a loss amid the high cost of fuel.
“Nagbawas po kami ng kaunting biyahe. Nag-iipon muna po kami ng mga pasahero,” Victory Liner terminal master Ariel Santos said.
(We have reduced some trips to allow more passengers to gather.)
“Kapag nakaipon na po kami ng mga 30 pasahero, doon pa lang po namin bubuksan ‘yung makina at ang aircon ng bus, tsaka doon pa lang po kami magpapasakay ng mga pasahero,” he added.
(Once we have around 30 passengers, that’s when we start the engine and turn on the air-conditioning, and only then do we allow passengers to board.)
The Department of Transportation (DOTr) has already met with interagency officials to formulate measures to address the looming fuel crisis.
Among the key measures discussed was a proposed public transport fare hike.

Meanwhile, stakeholders are still awaiting Malacañang's decision on the possible removal of excise taxes on petroleum products, especially with Dubai crude prices reaching US$123 per barrel, well above the US$80 threshold for tax relief intervention.

The DOTr has also approved an additional round of targeted relief assistance under the Department of Social Welfare and Development's (DSWD) Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situations (AICS) program.

“We are examining possible implementation arrangements. We will continue to advance social protection mechanisms to help affected transport workers,” DSWD spokesperson Assistant Secretary Irene Dumlao said. — Lyjah Tiffany Bonzo/MCG, GMA News

articles.title: MS Now says reporters denied access to White House after Trump media ban
articles.summary:
President said he was banning MS Now, CNN and Politico journalists, saying of their coverage: ‘You get sick of it.’

News outlet MS Now…

blocks.text: News outlet MS Now said its journalists were denied access to the White House grounds on Saturday morning, a day after Donald Trump said he would ban the news channel and two other news outlets, CNN and Politico, from the executive branch complex.
The outlet said a reporter and a cameraman had been denied access and had their White House press passes confiscated by the US Secret Service at a security gate outside the West Wing.

“The White House belongs to the American people and the decisions made inside are funded by our tax dollars,” MS Now said, adding that it “intends to take any and all steps necessary to defend our first amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy.
“We stand firmly behind our anchors, our reporters and our newsroom. We will continue to report on the president, the administration and the issues that impact the American people.”

Trump’s threat to banish CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House has brought condemnation from first amendment advocates and Democratic officials, among others, as the conflict between the US president and parts of the media sharply escalates ahead of November’s midterm elections. It has also thrown into stark relief Trump’s attack on press freedom in the US, which has unnerved civil liberties advocates.

In a Truth Social post on Friday afternoon, Trump said he would order the removal of the news outlets “effective immediately” for what he claimed was “constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” and said he is considering banning more. Trump did not identify a single infraction, but rather said his decision was “really just cumulative stories over the last two years. You get sick of it.”

The White House Correspondents’ Association, which represents the White House press corps, condemned the move. “The constitution protects the freedom of the press from government interference,” it said on social media. “That protection does not depend on whether the president likes a news organization’s coverage, agrees with its reporting or approves of the questions its journalists ask.”

The body said the issue is “about more than the rights of journalists” but about “the right of the American people to receive a full and independent account of the activities, policies and decisions of whoever occupies the nation’s highest office”.

Trump has long clashed with the media over what he considers slanted coverage of his administration and himself personally, as well as describing a media environment in which the press and his political opponents are in collusion.
Last year the Associated Press was banned form the White House after refusing to acknowledge an executive order changing the name of the Gulf of Mexico to Gulf of America.
After Friday’s ban was announced, CNN issued a statement saying that removing its reporters from the grounds could violate the law.
after newsletter promotion

“CNN stands fully behind our White House team and their fair and accurate reporting,” a spokesperson for the outlet said. “We have a right under the US constitution to do that reporting without hindrance or interference from the government.”

Politico also issued a statement, saying it would “continue to fairly report on this White House and future ones” and “will vigorously defend our first amendment rights against any attempt to restrict them”.

Jim Acosta, a former CNN reporter, accused Trump of “taking a meat axe to the free press in this country”. Speaking on MS Now on Friday, Acosta called the latest media bans “a slippery slope” and warned: “We are on the path to having a state media-like system in this country.”

Acosta said the media should collectively oppose Trump’s ban. “Each of these news organizations should sue the White House, sue Donald Trump, and that other news organizations in Washington should band together and say, ‘We will not go to the White House and cover you and cover your administration. We’re banning you.’”

Press freedom group PEN America said: “Someone needs to explain to President Trump how the first amendment works. As we’ve seen time and time again, this administration’s hostility toward the press is never about the accuracy of news stories, but about its inability to withstand scrutiny of its actions. The White House can’t be allowed to decide which journalists are able to cover the president based on the content of their news coverage.”

articles.title: Drone sightings briefly shut Luxembourg airport
articles.summary: Flights were diverted and hundreds of passengers affected after unauthorized drones appeared near Luxembourg's only international airport.

image.caption: Drone sightings forced Luxembourg's only international airport to briefly suspend flights overnight [FILE: August 11, 2026]Image: Steven Mohr/SNS/picture alliance

blocks.text: Luxembourg authorities are investigating drone sightings that forced the country's main airport to temporarily suspend flights overnight, Prime Minister Luc Frieden said on Saturday.
Frieden said Luxembourg was working with its NATO allies following the incident, which comes amid heightened European concern over suspected hybrid attacks linked to Russia.
What happened at Luxembourg airport?
National carrier Luxair said more than 1,800 passengers were affected, with 17 incoming flights diverted to airports including Brussels, Paris and Frankfurt.
Flights resumed on Saturday, although Luxair warned that delays and knock-on disruption could continue.
The airport said the closure was a precautionary measure to protect passengers, airline crews, airport employees and aircraft.
Frieden stressed that it was too early to determine who was responsible.
"We are analyzing the situation," Frieden told a televised press conference after an emergency meeting with the country's defense and interior ministers.
Have other drones been spotted?
Frieden said "potentially larger drones" had also been observed in Luxembourg's airspace in recent days.
"This is new for Luxembourg, but it is not completely new for our neighboring countries," he said.
Germany blames Russia for attempted terror attack in Leipzig
Unauthorized drones have previously been detected near sensitive sites elsewhere in Europe, including Belgium, Germany and Denmark.
"We will ensure, together with our partners, that we can guarantee the security of our populations," Frieden said.

European governments have repeatedly warned of Russian-linked hybrid activities since Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Such incidents have included suspected sabotage, cyberattacks and unauthorized drone flights.
There is currently no evidence establishing who was responsible for the Luxembourg sightings.

articles.title: Ombudsman Remulla: All barangay officials have pork barrel
articles.summary: Ombudsman Boying Remulla on Saturday criticized the current barangay system, saying it has supposedly paved the way for barangay officials to have their own pork barrel.

blocks.text: Published September 19, 2026 9:45pm
Ombudsman Boying Remulla on Saturday criticized the current barangay system, saying it has supposedly paved the way for barangay officials to have their own pork barrel.
Remulla said this was because barangay officials serve as frontline government personnel.
“We have to rethink the barangay system,” Remulla said.

Speaking on his radio program on dzRH, Remulla commented on the passage of a bill extending the terms of barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan (SK) officials, while questioning the qualifications required for the positions.
“Lahat sila, may pork barrel, hanggang konsehal ng SK,” Remulla said. (All of them have a pork barrel, even down to SK councilors.)
“May sariling pork barrel yang mga 'yan, lalo na yung mayayaman na cities at municipalities,” he added.
(They have their own pork barrel, especially in wealthy cities and municipalities.)

Remulla made the remark while discussing the Senate's recent approval of a measure seeking to extend the terms of barangay and SK officials from four years to five years. The measure was approved with 13 affirmative votes and five negative votes.
Sen. Francis “Chiz” Escudero, the bill's principal author and sponsor, said the extended term would give barangay and SK officials more time to implement programs.

“Barangays are planners, implementers, first responders, peacekeepers, and frontline service providers — all at a level where government interacts directly with households and families,” Escudero said.

During the program, Remulla asked Sen. JV Ejercito about the current qualifications for barangay officials. Ejercito said the requirements remained unchanged under the bill, including the ability to read and write.
Remulla then suggested that barangay officials, including barangay captains, should be required to have civil service eligibility.—MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Asian Games open in Nagoya with glitzy ceremony after troubled buildup
articles.summary: Organizers will hope the ceremony can draw a line under a rocky buildup laden with complaints from athletes and officials involving accommodation and transport

blocks.text: PHILIPPINE DELEGATION. Filipino athletes get ready to compete at the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan.
POC Media Pool
Organizers will hope the ceremony can draw a line under a rocky buildup laden with complaints from athletes and officials involving accommodation and transport

items: The 20th Asian Games opened in Nagoya with a colorful ceremony, despite facing operational issues and complaints from athletes regarding accommodations and logistics.
Emperor Naruhito declared the Games open, and the event featured a parade of 45 nations, with a heavy security presence and a theme of Asian solidarity.
While competitions have begun, tensions arose with incidents involving Taiwan and South Korea, overshadowing hopes for a peaceful Games.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
NAGOYA, Japan – The 20th Asian Games opened in Nagoya on Saturday with a glittering ceremony of dance and fireworks following a buildup marred by operational gaffes and logistical problems.

Five years after the Tokyo Olympics played out at empty venues due to COVID-19 restrictions, Japan welcomed fans to the Mizuho Park Athletic Stadium for a curtain-raiser that was initially subdued before bursting into a festival of colour and sound.
Emperor Naruhito declared the Games open after watching the parade of 45 nations and regions at a dignitaries’ table along with International Olympic Committee boss Kirsty Coventry.
Naruhito’s visit with royal family members was accompanied by a heavy security operation. Organizers had said up to 10,000 police would be deployed for the ceremony.

“While the world is too often divided by conflict, they (the Asiad athletes) remind us that sport remains a powerful force for peace, understanding and friendship among nations,” Olympic Council of Asia President Sheikh Joaan bin Hamad Al Thani said in a speech.

Japan’s father-and-son duo of Shigenobu Murofushi and Koji Murofushi, both former Asian Games champions in hammer throw, jointly lit the cauldron after climbing a set of stairs at the end of the torch relay.
Organizers will hope the ceremony can draw a line under a rocky buildup laden with complaints from athletes and officials involving accommodation and transport.
Japan’s reputation for precision and efficiency has been under scrutiny as the nation welcomes more than 11,000 athletes competing for 369 gold medals in a whopping 43-sport programme.

Instead of building a dedicated Games village, organisers have housed the athletes and officials in a mix of hotel rooms, temporary wooden containers and a cruise ship docked in the bay as a cost-cutting measure.

Several national team delegations, including hosts Japan, have found the arrangements below par, complaining of mix-ups and double-bookings, while South Korea said the containers at Garden Pier were too cramped for their basketballers.
India’s powerful cricket board took matters into their own hands, arranging for the men’s star-studded cricket team to stay in a separate hotel due to a tight allocation of beds from organisers.
Delegations have also lamented long waits for the athletes registering on arrival and have found buses turning up late or sending their athletes to the wrong venues.
The Olympic Council of Asia, which runs the quadrennial Games, acknowledged the problems on Saturday but played them down as teething difficulties.

Directed by Yukihiko Tsutsumi, the opening ceremony made a low-key start, with classical music and dance on a heart-shaped stage before the parade of nations which featured a delegation from reclusive North Korea.
The spectacle ramped up later though, with dancers in boiler suits marking Nagoya’s manufacturing tradition and a fireworks display closing the night.
The ceremony’s theme was “Harmonic Heart Beat” — intended to communicate Asian solidarity at an event often riven by geopolitical tension and historic grudges.
However, hopes for a peaceful Games have already been undermined by several incidents.
Taiwan’s delegation temporarily refused to participate in their welcoming ceremony on Friday after sports minister and former Olympic champion Lee Yang was blocked from attending it.
The South Korean men’s hockey team were upset when North Korea’s national anthem was played at the stadium before a match instead of their own.
While competitions for basketball, soccer and other sports have already started, the first gold medal will be won on Sunday, likely in the triathlon.
A high-class swimming competition kicks off in Tokyo on Sunday, with the programme featuring China’s 100 metres freestyle world-record holder Pan Zhanle and 13-year-old sensation Yu Zidi.
Apart from traditional Olympic sports, the Games will stage regional favourites kabaddi and sepak takraw along with quirky, modern events.

Esports will award medals again after making its debut at Hangzhou, while teqball, a mix of table tennis and soccer, and “virtual taekwondo” will make their first appearance at the Games. – Rappler.com

articles.summary: The police have since set up a task team to investigate the murders and have urged women in the Kempton Park area to avoid walking or running alone "particularly in isolated areas".

blocks.text: Runners gathered in South Africa to pay tribute to Elizabeth Moselakgomo after her body was found east of Johannesburg.
She is one of nine women found in the Kempton Park area, since July.
The jogger, known as "Tsontso", went missing during a routine run.
Runners organised an event in city of Centurion to honour her and defend women's right to run freely.
"This is for her - we just want to live and go running and come back home without having to think that it may be one of us", said Nonhle Mpohlo.
In Cape Town, people gathered in a vigil to honour the victims and called on the government to act.
The police have since set up a task team to investigate the murders and have urged women in the Kempton Park area to avoid walking or running alone "particularly in isolated areas".

articles.title: Greenland, Denmark say US deal will not cede sovereignty
articles.summary: Denmark and Greenland assure sovereignty in US military deal, aiming to enhance Arctic security while respecting self-determination amidst Trump's controversial claims.

blocks.text: DENMARK. Denmark's Minister of Defense Jeppe Bruus, along with Greenland's Minister for Foreign Affairs Mute B. Egede, visits the NATO military exercise Arctic Shield 2026 in Narsarsuaq, Greenland, on Wednesday, September 9, 2026
Photo from Ritzau Scanpix/Mads Claus Rasmussenvia/Reuters
Denmark and Greenland assure sovereignty in US military deal, aiming to enhance Arctic security while respecting self-determination amidst Trump's controversial claims.

items: Denmark and Greenland reaffirmed that any agreement with the United States will not compromise Greenland's sovereignty, despite President Trump's claims of 'permanent control' over the island's security.

A new agreement is set to allow the US to establish a significant military presence in Greenland while preventing adversaries from building bases there, with details about the extent of this presence still unclear.

Both Denmark and Greenland expressed optimism that the upcoming deal, expected to be signed during the UN General Assembly, will enhance security in the Arctic while respecting the sovereignty of the Danish kingdom.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

COPENHAGEN, Denmark – Denmark and Greenland on Saturday said any agreement with the United States would not compromise Greenland’s sovereignty, after President Donald Trump said the deal would give Washington “permanent control” over the Arctic island’s security, leaving its precise scope unclear.

The United States, Denmark and Greenland said late on Friday they had entered into an agreement for the US to ‌develop a significant military presence on Greenland, while prohibiting US adversaries from building their own bases on the island.

Key details of the agreement have not been made public, including the degree of US military presence in the self-governed ⁠Danish territory and whether any formal power over foreign policy and resources would be ceded to Washington.

Denmark and Greenland expressed hope that a deal, which is expected to be signed during the UN General Assembly next week, would end months of uncertainty triggered by Trump’s threats to seize control of Greenland.
“Next week could be a good week – for Greenland, Denmark, and the United States,” Denmark’s Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen said in a statement posted on Facebook on Saturday.

“A time of uncertainty will hopefully give way to a binding agreement that strengthens security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic, and thereby our shared security within NATO and Europe — while respecting the (Danish) Kingdom’s red lines,” he said.
Denmark and Greenland have repeatedly insisted that Washington respect the sovereignty of the Danish kingdom and accept that Greenland is not for sale.

Trump said on Truth Social late on Friday that under a deal, “the United States will FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the security of Greenland, and the United States of America.”

The deal “gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland,” Trump said, adding that no adversary would ever be permitted to have a base or military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments there, without Washington’s express written approval.
Trump made the announcement after Reuters exclusively reported that the US and Denmark were closing in on a deal.

“I am pleased on Greenland’s behalf that we are nearing the conclusion of an agreement — an agreement that benefits not only our collective security but also the continued development of this country,” Greenland’s Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said on Saturday in a post on Facebook.
“The agreement recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of our Kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination,” he added.
Trump’s threats, which peaked in January, triggered a diplomatic crisis that strained relations within NATO and pushed Denmark and Greenland into negotiations aimed at defusing the pressure.
A NATO spokesperson on Saturday said the alliance welcomed the agreement, which would “help advance security, stability and cooperation in this vital region.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: Thousands protest Kennedy Center demolition fears
articles.summary: Protesters took part in a "Hands Around the Kennedy Center" human chain. The demonstration comes amid fears the Trump administration could tear the arts hub down.

image.caption: Protesters joined hands to form a human chain around the venueImage: J. Scott Applewhite/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Thousands of people have demonstrated at the Kennedy Center in Washington D.C. amid fears President Donald Trump's administration could demolish the arts hub.
Crowds of people gathered in the Foggy Bottom area of the US capital city, many carrying signs as they joined in "Hands Around the Kennedy Center."
Some of those gathered held hands and formed a human chain around the center.
Protesters waved placards reading "hands off Kennedy Center" and sang songs close to where workers removed Trump's name from the building in June following a court order.

blocks.caption: Actor Lynda Carter, a vocal Trump critics, addressed the rally on FridayImage: Jose Luis Magana/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Protesters, residents condemn move to demolish Kennedy Center
"It makes me sick to my stomach," the AFP news agency quoted Neal Racioppo, a Washington resident who runs marketing and communications for a theatre, as saying.
Trump "can't get his name on this cherished building, so he is depriving the world of what it could be."
"He does not have a right to decide that an institution, a living memorial to a past president, can be demolished," another protester told AFP.
"The Kennedy Center is vital to the arts in Washington. We need it. We need this,” said local arts community member Bud Wilkinson.
"This is not just about putting the president's name on the Kennedy Center. It's about censoring the performances and the programming," Wilkinson said.
Trump and the Kennedy Center
The Kennedy Center — inaugurated in 1971 following the assassination of US President John F. Kennedy — has been a focal point of Trump's plans for Washington since 2025.
Trump has been pushing for major renovations and claims the building was left in a severe state of disrepair by those previously in control.
Trump's handpicked Kennedy Center board voted last year to rename the institution the Trump-Kennedy Center.
In May, a judge ruled that his name was illegally added and ordered it removed.

blocks.caption: The Kennedy Center board voted last year to rename the institution the Trump-Kennedy CenterImage: Cliff Owen/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: What has Trump said about the Kennedy Center?
On Wednesday, Trump appeared to imply that the Kennedy Center could be torn down if his administration did not receive "recognition."

"For the Trump administration, for me to get involved and to take that on long term and to carry it or to raise money to carry it, I think that the Trump administration should certainly have recognition, because frankly, if we don't do that, it's going to close," Trump said.
"It'll end up being ripped down. It's in very, very bad shape, very dangerous shape," Trump told reporters.

articles.title: There might be no economic case for expanding the Port of Churchill, but that may not be the point
articles.summary: The question before Manitobans right now is why Canada and Manitoba are not simply proceeding with a $3-billion port expansion and railway upgrade, if indeed a Hudson Bay shipping route is essential…

image.caption: The Port of Churchill, in northern Manitoba, must be modernized before it can ship higher volumes of commodities.s. (CBC)

blocks.text: Manitoba·Analysis

The question before Manitobans right now is why Canada and Manitoba are not simply proceeding with a $3-billion port expansion and railway upgrade, if indeed a Hudson Bay shipping route is essential for Canadian sovereignty.
Canada might need shipping route as sovereignty insurance policy, even if it pays a premium to do so
Piece by piece, like patches of ice receding from a frigid waterway, Manitoba's plan to expand the Port of Churchill is getting clearer.

Late last week, port owner Arctic Gateway Group attached a price range to the task of upgrading the site and the railway that connects it to the rest of Canada. CEO Chris Avery said it would cost $2 billion to $3 billion to expand the port to allow it to ship higher volumes of commodities and rebuild the Hudson Bay Railway so it can carry heavier loads.
In the context of provincial megaprojects, $3 billion is nowhere near unprecedented. There are two other projects in the works in Manitoba right now that are in the same price range.

The upgrades underway to the largest of Winnipeg's three sewage-treatment plants are expected to cost $3.2 billion once they're finished. The City of Winnipeg has assembled most of the money it needs to complete the job, which is entering its final phase.

The proposed expansion of Manitoba Hydro's gas-burning generating station in Brandon is also expected to cost $3 billion. Pending regulatory approval, the Crown corporation is ready to proceed with buying three new natural gas turbines.

The Port of Churchill expansion, meanwhile, exists in some sort of development limbo. The essential $3-billion work was not the subject of any pitch at Prime Minister Mark Carney's investment summit in Toronto this week.

Rather, the upgrades to the port and railway exist as a precursor to a larger project touted by Premier Wab Kinew — a $79-billion port expansion that includes a liquefied natural gas terminal floating off the shore of Hudson Bay.

items: Port of Churchill, railway improvements would cost fraction of LNG project proposed by Manitoba premier

blocks.text: The question before Manitobans right now is, why is the province not simply proceeding with a $3-billion port expansion and railway upgrade, if indeed this infrastructure is a prerequisite for other projects that are inevitable?
The answer is that the provincial government still has a choice as to whether it wishes to proceed.

The City of Winnipeg didn't have a choice when it pulled the trigger on upgrades to its North End Water Pollution Control Centre. Without those upgrades, Winnipeg would violate its environmental licence, run out of sewage-treatment capacity and end up unable to approve new residential and industrial development.

Manitoba Hydro, meanwhile, contends it is also in a difficult position. Without three more gas turbines in place in Brandon by 2030, Hydro argues, Manitobans could suffer from mid-winter power shortages.

There is less at stake if Manitoba dawdles on Churchill, as failing to upgrade the port and railway would affect far fewer residents. The town and dozens of other northern Manitoba communities stand to benefit the most from this particular megaproject.

As well, the economic benefits of the port expansion have not been demonstrated. The federal government has thus far refused to publish a Port of Churchill market sounding it commissioned. This raises suspicion international markets are not in love with the idea.

This could be why Kinew appears to be more interested in pursuing a liquefied natural gas moonshot. This week, the premier said this much larger project provides potential backers with a greater potential rate of return.
All of this ignores the primary purpose Canada ought to be interested in expanding the port at this moment in history, when our American friends have proven to be less than friendly.

As some of the world's leading experts in supply chains have stated over the past year, the Port of Churchill is of vital importance to Canada as an insurance policy — that is, an alternative means of getting goods out of the country — as opposed to being a money-maker.
Avery made this point last week, effectively arguing the port must be expanded if Canada ever hopes to divert more exports away from the United States.

"If we want to grow our non-U.S. trade by 10 percentage points, that's the equivalent volume of four times the size of the Port of Vancouver. So that gives you a context of what we're looking at,'" he said in an interview.

To be clear, Avery has never said an expanded Port of Churchill won't make money. But there is an argument to be made that its value as an insurance policy — effectively, the Canadian sovereignty argument — ought to make its potential as an economy-transforming revenue source a secondary concern.
University of British Columbia transportation and logistics professor Trevor Heaver said in 2025 that Canada should expand the Port of Churchill even without a purely economic case to do so.

items: 1st phase of Winnipeg's $3.2B North End sewage treatment plant upgrade nearing completion
Manitoba Hydro critics fuelled by data showing gas plant underperforms during winter cold snaps

blocks.text: "You've got to view these things from a national perspective, and that is present in this route," said Heaver, adding that insurance, by definition, comes at a higher cost.
Higher costs are certain for a route that involves an isolated port operated in frigid conditions on water that requires ice-hardened vessels to navigate for at least seven months out of the year.

"The economics may play out that it doesn't pay financially, commercially. So then, you're left with the issue of how much are you prepared to pay for the resilience, and how much are you prepared to pay for the sovereignty which comes from it?" Heaver said.
“How much are you prepared to pay for the revitalization of northern Manitoba?”

Heaver is not alone. Vidya Mani, a University of Virginia professor who studies global supply chains, said the Port of Churchill offers Canada's international trade partners the clear benefit of a shipping route that's free of geopolitical conflict.
She said the question is not whether Hudson Bay shipping offers Canada more flexibility.

items: Canada and the EU are getting cosy. These charts show how our economies stack up
The journey toward an expanded Port of Churchill has only just begun

blocks.text: "It is more a question of, can this flexibility be paid for?" Mani asked. "It will cost, but can you pay for it?"
Right now, no one's lining up to pay that $3-billion bill. The province doesn't have the ability to do so on its own.

While Manitoba Hydro and the City of Winnipeg can rely on utility bills to finance their own $3-billion projects, the province has no self-sustaining revenue source of its own to tap for a Churchill megaproject.
It's also burdened with nearly $40 billion of its own debt.

items: Manitoba sought U.S. help to develop large AI data centre and find private financial partner on $18B hydro dam

blocks.text: Documents obtained by CBC News show the Manitoba government sought U.S. advice last year to find private partners to build an artificial intelligence data centre near Winnipeg, as well as a new Nelson River hydro station, without affecting the province's own balance sheet.
While those talks didn't appear to go anywhere, the mere fact Manitoba was looking for private partners to pay for megaprojects is revealing.
Arctic Gateway can't foot the Churchill tab, either. It's owned by First Nations and other northern communities.
This leaves the federal government as the only saviour if Kinew's trip to Toronto this week did not result in big money coming to the Port of Churchill's rescue.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Bartley Kives joined CBC Manitoba in 2016. Prior to that, he spent three years at the Winnipeg Sun and then 18 at the Winnipeg Free Press, writing about politics, music, food and outdoor recreation. He's the author of three books — two of them Canadian bestsellers — and the winner of a Canadian Screen Award for reporting.

articles.title: Family of Bhishma Rajyaguru, killed in crash with Sask. Roughrider, mourns his death
articles.summary: Bhishma Rajyaguru's father and sister remember him after he died when ​Saskatchewan Roughrider​ Jayden Dalke crashed into his vehicle.

image.caption: Bhishma Rajyaguru, 22, died in a fatal crash with Saskatchewan Roughrider Jayden Dalke near Lumsden, Sask., on July 18. (Submitted by Dakshesh Raval)

blocks.text: Saskatchewan
Bhishma Rajyaguru's father and sister remember him after he died when ​Saskatchewan Roughrider​ Jayden Dalke crashed into his vehicle.
Family remembers Rajyaguru as aspirational and musically gifted
“Happy birthday, Papa.”
Those were Bhishma Rajyaguru’s last words to his dad, Ashish Rajyaguru.
It was a 15-second call from more than 11,000 kilometres away. Ashish wishes he could make the call longer and the distance shorter.
“We were calling him in the morning, but he didn’t pick up,” Ashish said.
“Why I didn't talk to him [longer]? What is he doing? Where is he going? I just wanted to know.”

Bhishma, 22, ​​died​ on July 18 after ​Saskatchewan Roughrider​ Jayden Dalke crashed into his vehicle. The CFL player was driving the wrong way on a divided highway, with cannabis and alcohol in his SUV, according to RCMP.
Both Dalke and Bhishma were pronounced dead at the scene.
“We couldn’t believe it. We lost everything,” Ashish said. “We were just mourning and crying. We were just crying and crying.”

items: Friends, family mourn 22-year-old killed in wrong-way crash near Lumsden, Sask.
Sask. Roughrider in fatal crash was driving on wrong side of divided highway: RCMP

blocks.text: Bhishma came to Canada as a student in April 2022. He had not been home since. Ashish remembers the airport goodbye: waving through a window pane, trying to hide his worried frown under an assuring smile and hoping to see Bhishma again soon.
“I told him to focus totally on education and make a bright career over there," Ashish said. "His dreams were very powerful and he was very aspirational.”

Ashish's morning walks are quieter now. He misses Bhishma's chatter. Ashish remembers his son saying on one of those walks that he wanted to become famous enough for Google to feature a personalized snippet whenever people looked him up.
“Bhishma’s name shows up on Google now, but he’s no more,” Ashish said in Gujarati.

Bhishma died a month away from Rakshabandhan, an Indian festival celebrating the relationship between brothers and sisters. As part of the Indian custom and festivities, a sister ties a colourful thread to her brother’s wrist as a symbol of mutual love and respect.

For the last four years Bhishma’s sister, 19-year-old Hir Rajyaguru, had been pretend-tying the bracelet over video calls. Hir said Bhishma promised her during last year’s exchange that he would be physically present for this year’s celebrations.
At this year's festival, Hir tied the bracelet to Bhishma’s lifeless wrist as he lay in a casket.
“It will be the hardest day of every year for me,” she said.
“He always used to make me laugh and always used to make fun of me in an annoying way. But secretly, I loved it, because he was my brother and that is what I loved about him.”
Bhishma Rajyaguru's sister speaks about the pain of losing her brother
When RCMP called to notify the family of Bhishma’s death, Hir answered the phone.
“I couldn't believe anything. I told my father that I think that this is a fraud call, you should not talk to him.”
It took more than two weeks for Bhishma’s body to reach India after autopsies and tests. In the meantime, the family could only access him through photos and videos.
“[Even] after seeing the photos [of Bhishma’s body], we used to believe that he might be sleeping. He will wake up. He will wake up,” Hir said.
LISTEN | Friend says it 'means a lot' to see crash victim Bhishma Rajyaguru honoured before Roughriders game:
The 30613:38Friends mourn death of Bhishma Rajyaguru after crash near Lumsden
Bhishma’s friends remember him as a talented musician and a 3 a.m. friend — somebody they could always count on.

Bhishma was a percussionist in a Regina-based band. His band members say he had been looking forward to playing at Garba in the Park, an event celebrating folk dance and music. The event, scheduled for July 25, was postponed out of respect for Bhishma and his friends and family.
Even though Bhishma's instrument has gone silent, Hir continues to hum what her brother would play. She says Bhishma’s legacy will live on in the tunes he left behind and the smiles he inspired.
“He always wanted everyone to laugh in the hardest time. Everyone should keep smiling,” Hir said.
“Anytime my parents are grieving about him, or they cry, I always tell them that if my brother was here, he would have never liked to see you guys cry this much.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Based in Regina, Shlok Talati is a reporter with CBC Saskatchewan. Talati joined CBC News as a Donaldson Scholar in 2023. He has since worked with The World This Hour, CBC Toronto's digital desk, and CBC Sask. He holds a master of journalism from the University of King's College, Halifax. You can reach him at shlok.talati@cbc.ca

articles.title: Jim Ratcliffe says the UK is a country ‘on the slide’
articles.summary:
Co-owner of Manchester United says Britain is in decline because of high taxes and immigration

The co-owner of Manchester United Sir Jim Ratcliffe has described the UK as being a country “on…

blocks.text: The co-owner of Manchester United Sir Jim Ratcliffe has described the UK as being a country “on the slide” from the days when it had “the greatest empire in the world.”
Ratcliffe, who founded petrochemicals giant Ineos, and has resided in Monaco, which has a relaxed tax regime, since 2020, said Britain is in decline because of high taxes and immigration.

Ratcliffe’s latest attack on the UK comes seven months after he told Sky News that the country was being “colonised by immigrants”. He subsequently said he was sorry if those remarks had “offended some people”.
The billionaire told the BBC’s Big Boss Interview he believed the UK was in decline from the days when, he said, “we were a great people.”

He said: “We had the greatest empire in the world. We were a great people. We won two world wars. We’re good, honest folk. But unfortunately, at the moment, I think the UK is on the slide. It’s quite difficult to see how we arrest it.”
Ratcliffe also said the UK had “a bit of a green eye towards wealth at the moment”, “encouraging” the wealthiest to relocate.
He told the podcast: “In America, they applaud people who create wealth.

“And the good thing about those people who create wealth is that they then spend that wealth in the economy in which they’re resident. And, unfortunately, with the things that they’ve been doing, they’ve been encouraging the people who have created wealth to leave the UK because it’s just become uncomfortable for them for tax reasons or whatever.

While the UK’s tax burden has risen to its highest level since the second world war at about 35.3% of GDP, the Office for Budget Responsibility says it remains well below the average of 14 western European economies.

Ratcliffe has also been at odds with Manchester United fans over the summer after the club embarked on a major ticket-touting crackdown that ultimately revoked 685 season tickets, prompting protests from United supporter groups like the 1958.
The businessman was already fiercely unpopular among the Old Trafford faithful, ever since he decided to hike ticket prices and sack 450 club employees.

The billionaire also took aim at the government’s decision not to invest further in North Sea resources by granting licences for the Jackdaw and Rosebank oil and gasfields, which he said amounted to “insanity”, and warned the UK’s reliance on energy imports meant the country could “run out of gas” if there was a cold spell this winter.
after newsletter promotion

He said: “The risk you’ve got this winter is that we run out of gas. If we have a really sharp cold spell, then there is conceivably the possibility that we’ll run out of gas and have to switch the industry off.”
In response to the billionaire’s criticism, the government said it was working to deliver growth and that business investment had increased in the last two years.
A spokesperson told the BBC that they did not foresee any problems with gas supply: “We have a diverse energy mix and are confident in our security of supply.”
Asked if he was planning on returning to the UK, Ratcliffe said: “Not at the moment, no. I don’t see growth being tackled.
“Two things: we need politicians who are tough enough to deal with some very difficult problems, and we know what the problems are.
“And we need politicians who will make decisions which are good for the country, not good for themselves and their party. And we haven’t had one of those for a long time.”

articles.title: Millions without power as Cuba hit by latest major blackout
articles.summary: Widespread power outages have become increasingly common due to fuel shortages made worse by a US blockade.

blocks.text: Millions in Cuba were left without power on Friday as the country was plunged into yet another major blackout.
The country's entire electricity grid suffered "total disconnection" that triggered a nationwide outage, Cuba's energy ministry said.
Power was restored to some priority areas by late evening, including those near hospitals and water pumping stations in the capital Havana, grid operator UNE said.

It is at least the sixth partial or total blackout to hit Cuba this year, where ageing electricity infrastructure and chronic fuel shortages have been placed under further strain by a US blockade on oil shipments to the communist-run nation.
UNE said the outage started just before 14:00 local time on Friday (18:00 GMT) due to a transmission fault coupled with poor weather conditions in central Cuba.
Protocols to begin the "gradual restoration" of power were activated, the operator's national load dispatch director Felix Estrada said, with the process ongoing on Saturday.
Cuba relies heavily on fuel imports, meaning tight US sanctions and an oil blockade since the start of the year have exacerbated existing shortages.
Food and medicine have also become more scarce, with hospitals struggling to function normally and schools and government offices having to close.
"Lately, it's becoming a habit," Havana resident Frank Lorenzo told news agency Reuters on Friday.
"Before it happened less frequently - once a month… just yesterday we were 24 hours without electricity, they turned it on for just an hour and it went down again."
"It's one thing after another: no water, no gas for cooking, no electricity," 36-year-old schoolteacher Lidia Fernandez told news agency AFP. "Honestly, I don't know how we haven't gone crazy."
Francisco Rodriguez, 78, said his home had already gone without power for 28 hours on Friday and feared he would not have light "for several days".
The repeated blackouts have prompted rare protests in Cuba, where unauthorised demonstrations are illegal and those who defy the ban risk being jailed.

Havana has blamed its fuel crisis on the Trump administration and denounced all of its sanctions - including a new round announced in August - which are part of a wider pressure campaign against the Caribbean island's leadership.

Cuba's regional ally Venezuela was believed to have sent it around 35,000 barrels of oil a day - about half of its oil needs - until Venezuela's own supplies were cut off following the US seizure of its President Nicolás Maduro in January.
US President Donald Trump has threatened tariffs on countries shipping oil to Havana, and a number of such shipments have been seized by the US.

Washington meanwhile attributes Cuba's energy crisis to poor internal management and has accused it of posing a "national security threat". Trump has openly discussed toppling its leadership, including threatening a "friendly takeover" in March this year.

articles.title: Boying Remulla eyes revival of investment ombudsman
articles.summary: Ombudsman Jesus Crispin "Boying" Remulla said Saturday his office was planning to establish an investment ombudsman tasked to address concerns of business leaders.

blocks.text: Published September 19, 2026 6:02pm
Ombudsman Jesus Crispin "Boying" Remulla said Saturday his office was planning to establish an investment ombudsman tasked to address concerns of business leaders.
Speaking on his weekly radio program, Remulla discussed with his co-hosts the various ways how government processes burden different stakeholders.
The discussion raised that many business leaders and groups were hesitant to invest because of political instability—so whatever businesses are already operating should have fewer requirements.
Remulla called for the lessening the requirements for businesses, saying this may lead to more jobs for Filipinos.
"Magtatayo kami ng… investment ombudsman (We will establish an investment ombudsman)," Remulla said on radio station dzRH.
With such a government position in place, entrepreneurs would be able to go to the investment ombudsman if they have complaints at the barangay level or higher.
The investment ombudsman is an old post, with multiple administrations attempting to revive the post to curb corruption in the procurement of business permits from the government.
In 2007, then-Trade secretary Peter Favila attempted to place an investment ombudsman within the Department of Trade and Industry.
Remulla said efforts were already underway to hire more lawyers for the effort.
"We're hiring 61 more lawyers ngayon hanggang December, then next year, we will hire 100 or 200 more," Remulla said.
(We're hiring 61 more lawyers now until December, then next year, we will hire 100 or 200 more.)
Remulla admitted that there were issues with agencies such as the Anti-Red Tape Authority and the Philippine Competition Commission, but did not elaborate. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Oktoberfest 2026: Everything you need to know
articles.summary: This year, AI will be used to manage overcrowded situations. Find all the numbers surrounding the fest — including the price of water!

image.caption: Oktoberfest attracts millions of visitors every yearImage: Wolfgang Maria Weber/IMAGO

blocks.text: On Saturday, September 19, at noon, Oktoberfest will once again open with the ceremonial tapping of the keg, during which the mayor of Munich drives a tap into the first wooden barrel of beer and calls out "O'zapft is," a Bavarian phrase that translates to "It's tapped."
His call will be followed by 12 gunshots, a signal that lets all festival tents know that they can start serving beer.
More than 6 million people are expected at the world's largest Volksfest, which runs this year through October 4.
Oktoberfest: What to know about 'the best party in Germany'
Expanded security measures to prevent overcrowding
The festival grounds are enormous: Oktoberfest takes place on Munich's Theresienwiese, a 34.5-hectare site roughly the size of 48 soccer fields.
But crowds can swell, especially on weekends — sometimes to dangerous levels.
Last year, officials had to temporarily close the entrances.

One reason is that nearly all 38 beer tents operate in two or three reservation shifts. When one group of guests leaves and the next arrives at the 14 large tents — which each accommodate several thousand people — huge numbers of visitors end up trying to enter and exit at the same time.
That's how, on one Saturday afternoon at last year's Oktoberfest, the crowds became so dense that movement temporarily came to a standstill. The crush caused some visitors to panic.
To prevent that from happening again, the city of Munich has overhauled its security plan for this year's festival.
Twenty-six new cameras, in addition to 56 police cameras, will monitor the grounds, while an AI system will analyze visitor flows and issue alerts if areas become overcrowded.

blocks.caption: Around 300,000 people were at Oktoberfest simultaneously on the second Saturday of the festival in 2025Image: Frank Hoermann/SVEN SIMON/picture alliance

blocks.text: A newly established coordination center is also intended to improve communication between security agencies and event organizers.
Organizers and police have drawn up a plan to defend against drones over the grounds, though no details have been disclosed.
In addition, 600 police officers will be deployed on site.
Oktoberfest is famous worldwide, but most visitors are local
Oktoberfest may be known around the world as an international tourist attraction, but most of its visitors don't travel very far to get there.
A study commissioned by the city of Munich last year found that the festival remains overwhelmingly regional.

blocks.caption: Statistically speaking, two international guests sit at every 10-person table in the festival tentsImage: Maryam Majd/REUTERS

blocks.text: In 2025, 41% of visitors came from Munich, another 25% from the surrounding area and 9% from elsewhere in the region. In all, three-quarters of Oktoberfest's roughly 6.5 million visitors came from Bavaria. Another 4% came from elsewhere in Germany.

About 21% of visitors — roughly 1.35 million people — traveled from abroad. Americans made up the largest group of international visitors, accounting for just under 20% of the total, or more than 270,000 people. Italians were next, at just over 13%.
Beer prices rise again
Cannabis is banned throughout the festival grounds.

Alcohol, on the other hand, is available in whatever quantities visitors are willing — and able — to pay for. A Mass, the traditional 1-liter mug of beer served at Oktoberfest, costs between €14.80 and €15.90 ($17-$18.25) this year, only slightly more than last year.
A liter of table water comes in at a hefty €11, although the grounds also have several free drinking water fountains.
Visitors planning to enjoy one of Oktoberfest's many rides would be wise to stay relatively sober. Tickets cost anywhere from just under €5 to €14.

Germany's traditional fairground culture was officially added to the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2026, and that tradition remains very much alive at the 191st Oktoberfest. According to organizers, about 90% of the festival's more than 130 fairground operators can trace their roots back to the 19th century.
The festival remains decidedly traditional when it comes to payment, too: Many vendors still accept cash only. Visitors caught without any can withdraw money from ATMs on the grounds.
Dirndl or lederhosen for Oktoberfest?
Then there's the question of what to wear.
Bavarians who take pride in doing things properly generally show up in local traditional dress.

blocks.caption: Traditional garb can be seen at the annual breweries' paradeImage: Felix Hörhager/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The dirndl is the traditional dress worn by women and girls, which consists of close-fitting bodice with a low neckline, a blouse worn under the bodice, a wide high-waisted skirt and an apron.
Men wear lederhosen, the traditional leather shorts or knee-length breeches with suspenders.

For those who are not Bavarian, lederhosen and dirndls are certainly an option, but they're by no means required. Munich's event marketing department, Simply Munich, advises first-time visitors to consider renting traditional garb rather than buying it.

Be aware that locals find cheap imitations of traditional dress off-putting, as Simply Munich points out: "If you want to avoid wry looks, steer clear of Seppl hats, 'leather pants' made of cloth and garish mini plastic dirndls. With jeans and a checkered shirt, you'll definitely be more suitably dressed."
This article was originally written in German.
