articles.title: Deadly shark attack prompts rare kill order in Western Australia
articles.summary: Police boats and helicopters are patrolling Perth's beaches as authorities continue their search for the swimmer's body, and the shark that attacked him.

blocks.text: A rare catch-and-kill order has been issued for a great white shark off the coast of Western Australia, after a man was killed while on a morning swim at a popular beach on Friday. His body has still not been found.
Authorities have said that beaches along the state's coast, including in the capital Perth, will remain closed until at least Sunday as the search for the shark continues.
It is the second shark attack in Western Australia (WA) this week, and the third fatal attack in the state this year.
The incident, at Sorrento Beach in Perth's north, has reignited debate about how to keep beachgoers safe in Australia.
The swimmer has been identified as 63-year-old Greg O'Neill, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC) has reported.
"Greg loved the ocean and was known as a passionate swimmer, sports lover, dedicated worker and an all-round generous, witty guy," his family said in a statement to the broadcaster.
Witness Jacqui Rapaic told the ABC that two men were swimming, but only one made it back to shore, and that she could see "a pool of blood" in the water.
Another witness told WAtoday that she saw the man being "mauled" as the shark "tossed him around like a fish".
Members of the public reported seeing a 2.5m-long (8ft 2in) shark at around the same time.
Authorities in Perth's Joondalup area, where Sorrento is located, said all beaches were closed "as a precautionary measure" and would remain so until at least midday on Sunday.
Pictures on Saturday showed the coastline being patrolled by a police boat and helicopter.
Catch-and-kill orders are rare and controversial in Australia, where great white sharks are a protected species.

WA Fisheries Minister Jackie Jarvis said that she took the "extraordinary step" of issuing the order after the shark was spotted by water police on Saturday morning, and "positively identified as the shark involved in the incident".
The minister said she authorised fisheries officers to "destroy the shark" if it could be captured because of the "exceptional circumstances" of the attack and the "hazard posed by the shark".
It is believed to be the first time in 10 years that such an order had been issued in WA, Jarvis added, emphasising that the order was not a widespread cull as the state has seen in the past.
The minister also said that the use of drones and tagging would be increased to help protect beachgoers.

Catching and killing sharks has a long and controversial history in Western Australia - there were months of huge protests in 2014 when the state government authorised a cull after a spate of attacks.

The incident in Sorrento is the second in WA this week - on Monday a 56-year-old man was bitten while surfing off the coast of Geraldton, 430km (270 miles) north of Perth. He survived but lost part of his leg, another surfer who rescued him told the ABC.
There have been five fatal shark attacks in Australia this year.

A 12-year-old boy died after he was bitten in Sydney Harbour in January, and three divers were fatally mauled in separate incidents between May and June - two in Western Australia and the third in Queensland.

articles.title: Rebels, workers, radicals: The making of 'Red Berlin'
articles.summary: Bloody May, student sit-ins and the squatter movement: Berlin has a long history as a hotbed for working-class organizing and radical left-wing politics.

image.caption: A Molotov cocktail explodes during the forced eviction of a squat in the Berlin district of Friedrichshain in 1990Image: Stefan Trappe/IMAGO

blocks.text: Berlin has a reputation for being unruly. When Jospeh Goebbels was appointed the Nazi Party's district leader in 1926, he described Berlin as "the reddest city in Europe besides Moscow." From the Tailors' Revolution of 1830 and the barricades of 1848, to the rise of a vast industrial working class later in the 19th century, revolution, protest and rebellion run deep throughout the city's history.

While the future German philosopher and revolutionary socialist Karl Marx was still in high school in the small town of Trier in Prussia's Rhine Province, Berlin was fast becoming a center of the country's labor movement. It was during the March Revolution of 1848 — a failed attempt to create a democratic German nation-state — that the General Workers' Brotherhood was founded, one of the first worker's organizations to become active in Germany.

blocks.caption: In March 1848, Berliners fought for basic freedoms and German unityImage: United Archives International/IMAGO

blocks.text: By the 1870s and 1880s, major industries from mechanical and railway engineering to ready-made clothing were located in the city. As the working-class population grew, this in turn impacted the city's political culture. "It became more populist in a positive sense: moving away from the traditional, elitist politics of the bourgeois liberals who had long dominated Berlin, and toward the inclusion of ordinary people, since at least men were now also important voters," Axel Weipert, a historian and author of the book "Red Berlin" (2019), tells DW.
Emergence of a radical labor movement

Berlin's labor movement became increasingly radical, partly in response to heavy-handed repression under the Chancellor Otto von Bismarck. Although Bismarck created the first modern welfare state to try and undercut the rising popularity of the socialist movement, he also introduced laws banning socialist and communist organizations, newspapers and public gatherings, as well as independent trade unions.

blocks.caption: A memorial to Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, who co-authored 'The Communist Manifesto' in 1848, still stands close to Berlin's city hallImage: Jürgen Ritter/IMAGO

blocks.text: After Bismarck resigned in 1890, the anti-socialist laws were repealed and the ideas of Karl Marx and his fellow revolutionary socialist Friedrich Engels became the ideology of what Weipert describes as a "genuine mass movement" in Berlin. The Social Democratic Party (SPD), Germany's oldest political party, was formed out of a merger between the General German Workers' Association and the social Democratic Workers' Party in 1875. Before World War I, the SPD was able to win far higher vote shares in Berlin than elsewhere in the country.

In 1914, the labor movement was seriously discredited when the SPD leadership and the trade unions decided not to oppose the war pushed by Kaiser Wilhelm II. But from 1916 onwards, Berlin became the center of mass labor strikes against the war. One of the earliest strikes was against the trial of anti-war socialist campaigner Karl Liebknecht. Together with Rosa Luxemburg and other left-wing radicals, Liebknecht founded the Spartacus League in Berlin, an underground group that later became the Communist Party of Germany (KPD).

blocks.caption: Karl Liebknecht (left) and Rosa Luxenburg were murdered by right-wing paramilitary soldiers of the Freikorps in BerlinImage: akg-images/picture-alliance

blocks.text: Triggered by war-weariness, severe food shortages and economic ruin, around half a million Berlin workers joined the January Strike of 1918. Supported by the Spartacus League, the anti-war strike was led by the Revolutionary Stewards, a clandestine network of factory workers and trade unions from large munitions and metal-working factories. The same group became a core organizing force behind the overthrow of the Kaiser in Berlin on November 9, 1918.
From left-wing unity to division

In the chaotic, war-torn city gripped by violent revolution, the Spartacist Uprising of 1919 was launched to overthrow Germany's provisional government and establish a republic of workers councils. Its violent suppression, which resulted in scores of deaths — Liebknecht and Luxemburg were both murdered by soldiers of right-wing paramilitary militias — permanently fractured the political left.

blocks.caption: Spartacist revolutionaries armed with machine guns aimed to establish a communist stateImage: Cola Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: As the capital of the newly founded Weimar Republic, Berlin remained a hotbed of radical politics in the interwar period. This was especially true in neighborhoods with large numbers of tenement buildings, such as Wedding, Kreuzberg and Neukölln, where thousands of factory workers lived in squalid conditions. The many large factories in Berlin also created shared interests and laid the groundwork for collective action.

"Bloody May" in 1929 saw brutal attacks on illegal May Day demonstrations which left at over 30 people dead. The SPD police president of Berlin had issued a ban on all public demonstrations for May Day, a ban defied by the KPD. In response, the police opened fire on protestors in the streets and also shot through windows in residential buildings, primarily in the working-class districts of Wedding and Neukölln.

blocks.caption: 'Bloody May' inspired the labor movement song 'Red Wedding' by Hanns Eisler and Erich WeinertImage: Atlantic Photo-Co/SVT/TT/IMAGO

blocks.text: During the Great Depression era, the SPD lost much of its support between 1929 and 1933, as joblessness ravaged the city. "Unemployment is critical — it meant that men were no longer attached to the SPD-led factory floor and trade union and the social bonds of these spaces and organizations," explains Pamela Swett, a historian at the University of Rhode Island. "Unmoored from the rhythm of daily life, men sought new bonds — new ways to feel self-respect and camaraderie with others." Some joined the KPD, which became known as the "Party of the Unemployed." Others joined far-right paramilitary groups such as the Nazi stormtroopers.
From student sit-ins to the housing crisis

After the Nazis took power in 1933, many of the labor movement leaders were killed or exiled. Then, in the aftermath of World War II, Berlin was divided into two separate political systems. East Berlin became the capital of the communist German Democratic Republic. Isolated from the Federal Republic of Germany, West Berlin deindustrialized, the labor movement weakened, and the SPD moved to the right.

During the Cold War, many left-leaning young men moved to West Berlin to evade military service. This intensified the student movement, the center of which was Berlin's Free University (Freie Universität). It was there, in leafy southwest Berlin, that historic sit-ins were held to protest the perceived authoritarianism of the government and the presence of former Nazi officials in positions of power. The fatal shooting of student Benno Ohnesorg by a police officer during a demonstration against the visiting Shah of Iran in 1967 radicalized a generation that led the widespread protests of 1968.

blocks.caption: The fatal shooting of student, Benno Ohnesorg, by police during protests against the Shah of Iran's visit in 1967 radicalized a generationImage: dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: In the early 1970s, a housing shortage led parts of the student movement but also apprentices and young migrant families to squat in West Berlin's empty buildings. "You have migrant laborers and young laborers participating, so this was part of working-class rebellion against capitalist housing," says Ralf Hoffrogge, a labor movement historian at Berlin's Free University.

Today, as gentrification sweeps the city, Berlin is home to the strongest and most radical tenants' movements in Germany. In a 2021 referendum, 59% of voters in the city approved the expropriation of property from private real-estate companies. Hoffrogge was part of the campaign, and his 2025 book "Loud Berlin" ("Das laute Berlin") explores how the housing crisis has become a catalyst for a "socialist renaissance" in the city. "It's not Berlin tenants against Berlin landlords, it's tenants against global capital. I think people have started to realize these contradictions and this is why class-based policy concepts are becoming popular again."

blocks.caption: 'Housing is not a commodity': Berlin's housing crisis and rapid gentrification have triggered new political initiatives in the cityImage: IPON/IMAGO

articles.title: Ed Sheeran continues US tour amid Palestinian controversy
articles.summary: Pro-Palestinian protests are expected at Ed Sheeran's first gig since Macklemore was dropped from the tour. The US rapper shouted "Free Palestine" at a concert in New Jersey.

image.caption: Sheeran's support acts said they were dropping out after Macklemore was removed [FILE: September 2024]Image: Carlos Elias Junior/Fotoarena/IMAGO

blocks.text: Pro-Palestinian protesters are expected to gather in Philadelphia on Saturday at Ed Sheeran's first show since US rapper Macklemore was removed from the tour for making Pro-Palestinian comments during a performance.
Sheeran, one of the best-selling musical artists of all time, has denied being responsible for dropping the US rapper from the lineup, saying that it was the promoter's decision to do so.
Ed Sheeran tour drops Macklemore after Gaza speech
Why was Macklemore dropped from Sheeran's tour?
Earlier this month, while performing at the opening of Sheeran's US Loop Tour in New Jersey, Macklemore expressed pro-Palestinian sentiments.

"One of the reasons why I wanted to come on this tour was because I wanted to stand up here on stages and stadiums across America and say two words that are very near and dear to my heart: 'Free Palestine.'"
Macklemore's comments were fiercely criticized by supporters of Israel in the US and led to him being dropped from the tour.
His removal from the billing sparked a backlash that saw support acts quitting and Sheeran facing a stream of criticism.
Sheeran's backing act, Irish folk band Beoga, announced they were leaving the tour. In an Instagram statement, they said they "fully supported" Macklemore's message.

blocks.caption: Macklemore, real name Benjamin Haggerty, was removed from the line-up over pro-Palestinian comments he made on stageImage: Jack Plunkett/Invision/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Sheeran says he is 'not complicit' in Macklemore's removal
Sheeran released a statement on Tuesday in which he laid out his apolitical stance on the matter.
"I am appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine. The suffering and pain caused on both sides is a human tragedy," Sheeran said.
The 35-year-old British performer said, "Upcoming tour dates had communicated that they would pull the shows if he was still supporting."
Sheeran added that American billionaire Robert Kraft, who owns Gillette Stadium near Boston where he was due to perform, was among those demanding Macklemore be cut from the tour.

"I am not complicit. I have my personal views on this devastating conflict. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn't mean I don't have them, and it doesn't mean I don't care," he said on Instagram on Tuesday.
"Those who come to my shows do not expect a political forum," the English singer-songwriter added.
Pro-Palestinian rally planned
Local groups have planned a pro-Palestinian rally near the concert venue on Saturday afternoon.
The AFP news agency cited local police as saying there would be an "appropriate police presence" to "help ensure the safety of concertgoers, employees and neighborhood residents."
Sheeran began his tour in Auckland, New Zealand in January and is set to wrap up in Mexico City in December, with shows still scheduled across North and South America.

articles.title: James Reid is finally home, and he’s right where he wants to be
articles.summary: James had spent much of his career feeling undeserving of all the recognition he was getting. But all along, there was really no need to strive to be anything more — and he would make that…

blocks.text: Sometime in 2010, a young, wide-eyed James Reid would exit the Pinoy Big Brother (PBB) house with more fame than he knew what to do with.

Within the walls of PBB, contestants would typically go months with no outside contact, but almost every move they made and every word they uttered was made known to everyone watching. And so, when the then-17-year-old Filipino-Australian emerged as the season’s Big Winner, hordes of people had come to celebrate him, much to his surprise.

Having just arrived in the Philippines, James hadn’t fully grasped what he had gotten himself into. He was timid, mostly spoke in English, and would, more often than not, merely flash a toothy grin in conversation with other housemates.

Still, he was immediately put on this pedestal and thrust under a spotlight he had no idea how to navigate. Fans would constantly assure him that there were plenty of reasons to love him, but the then-rising star didn’t feel worthy of any of that at all — even after topbilling film after film and giving life to songs (case in point: “Randomantic”) that have long found a permanent place in Filipino pop culture.

“I’ve just had such a backwards career where I already started with, at least in the Philippines, almost the maximum amount of fame without having done much to feel like I had deserved it or proven myself,” James told Rappler. “I just felt like a fraud in this whole industry. I’m not talking poorly of PBB or anything, but that’s the reality of the situation we get put in.”

Now 33, James is a completely different person. After taking a break from showbiz for six years to focus on other creative endeavors, he now carries himself with a greater sense of self-assurance, and no longer finds himself desperately searching for the feeling that he had earned the right to be where he stands now.
All along, there was really no need to strive to be anything more — and he would make that groundbreaking realization by fully diving into the music.

Make no mistake, though. James’ relationship with music hadn’t been perfect from the get-go either. It had gone through a noteworthy arc of its own, where he had felt restricted from displaying vulnerability and the liberty to write what he truly wanted.

“Definitely with past projects, I love the songs that I’ve made before, and I think there’s still a place for it in my life. But I can hear where I’m holding back. I can hear where I don’t want to go all the way or say too much or express myself too much because I know that one day it’s not going to be just in the studio, it’s going to be everywhere else,” James confessed.

This blatant display of openness used to scare the singer-actor. The creative process, he had once mentioned, is all him, but the minute it gets put on streaming platforms for the rest of the world to hear, the work no longer becomes his alone. It had taken a lot for James to get comfortable with that. But his genuine love for his craft had proven to be greater than any apprehensions he ever had. Now, he just sits back, lets his creativity flow, and just allows genuine inspiration to take over until it all builds up into something he can say he poured his whole soul into.

blocks.caption: James Reid

blocks.text: “I think that became so much of the point of all of it that I accepted it. So I didn’t really care about it anymore. And maybe that’s what made me feel more comfortable and more safe to just write whatever the hell I want to write about,” he shared.
This is something the “Pahinga” hitmaker truly makes evident in his latest creation, Honey I’m Home, a 10-track album that also happens to be his most personal body of work to date.

Most of it had been conceived at a songwriting camp in February 2025. It wasn’t anything glamorous, really — just James, some producers, writers, and artists making music in an open outdoor space uninterrupted, with nothing but a fan spinning above them.

“I just wanted to try something different where the creative process was not cut by people needing to go home because I feel like sometimes, you get into a groove, but then I get busy and I have to do some other thing. And then my mind and my heart is just not in the same place as it was that day. It’s difficult to bring things back,” he explained.
People came and went, but James remained there for two whole weeks, churning out the messiest of ideas until he finally began to strike gold.

At that point in time, it had only been a few months since James dropped his six-track EP jgh, which speaks of home in the physical sense. It was more of a compilation of random love songs he had put together after having just returned from traveling and being in the US, and overall feeling more grounded being back in the Philippines.

But in Honey, I’m Home, James speaks of love in an entirely new way. It’s not the kind of love you pull from watching romcoms — but the kind of love that feels so revolutionary it changes who you are and everything you’ve ever known about love. James credits all of that to his partner, Issa Pressman.

blocks.caption: James and Issa

blocks.text: “When we got together, she just had this different kind of kindness and light and warmth and generosity. I’ve never met anyone so in touch with their soul just naturally. It was inspiring, and not in the music sense, just me as a person. I’ve learned so much from her,” he said about Issa.

“And I think that gave me just a brand new perspective on how to love myself and how to love other people. In a much greater way than just chiming in some lyrics, I think the whole perspective of Honey, I’m Home came from the love that she gave me.”
There was a big change in James’ writing, and it all boils down to his change in perspective.

“Just the way I look at love, and the way I look at life, and the way that I see what I’m supposed to be doing here, I think my whole perspective shifted. And I think that’s the biggest thing that changed with the music,” he told Rappler.
With Honey I’m Home, then, you get a heavily layered record at its finest.

Take “Indiana” for instance. James and Issa have always dreamt of having a child of their own someday. The couple even already has a list of potential baby names, and one of them is Indiana. That’s how the song’s concept came to be in the first place: they already had so much love for a kid who wasn’t even born yet, and it was an indication of a love that transcends generations, time, and, eventually, death.

“I wanted to write it in a way where it says, ‘We love you so much, even though you’re not here. But also, we want you to know that far, far in the future when we’re gone, and you’re still here, that that love is still there,’” explained James. “And that made it extra hard, but I think I pulled it off. I imagine her still singing this song one day, even when I’m gone.”

blocks.caption: James offers ‘Indiana’ as a love letter to his future child with Issa.

blocks.text: In writing “Unbecoming,” meanwhile, James scrutinized every fiber of his being to determine which parts of himself he didn’t like anymore. It was a difficult yet absolutely necessary process he had to go through to fully describe how he’s changed after experiencing Issa’s love.
“[It’s the kind of love] that is not so much about what you give me, and is not so much about what I can give you. But the kind that changes my world and makes me a better person,” he said.

blocks.caption: James believes Issa helped him become a better person.

blocks.text: Yet the evolution isn’t just in the music itself, but in the village it took for all of this to happen. For the longest time, James was content with flying solo — doing all the work on his own, and even expressing reluctance toward the thought of having to rely on others to get things done.

When you look at the credits of Honey, I’m Home, you’ll be able to see that it was the product of consistent collaboration with other people. James attests that while it’s just his name on the record, it’s the hard work of those around him that made it all possible: his team at Careless, his producers Luke April and Brian Lotho, the featured artists on some of the tracks, and everyone else who contributed to the album in one way or another.
Above all, James is clearly no longer who he used to be.

blocks.caption: James is right where he’s meant to be. Photo by @henzonlyhope

blocks.text: “I think happy is probably the best word to use, so much so that I felt confident enough in myself that I could go back into the industry that caused me so much stress and anxiety before,” he said, referring to his first teleserye comeback in nearly a decade.
“I’m definitely in a place where I feel like I can just keep shooting for the stars and then seeing where things go. Because I feel like even if I fall, I have a nice place to land no matter what.”
And so, for as long as there is love to give and receive, James and his music are here to stay. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Mounties can now choose not to wear a name tag. A Halifax defence lawyer says that's a problem
articles.summary: A Halifax lawyer says an RCMP policy change that means officers are no longer required to wear name tags on their uniforms while on duty poses a threat to police accountability and transparency.

image.caption: A change in policy gives RCMP officers a choice in how they identify themselves on their uniforms. (RCMP)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia
A Halifax lawyer says an RCMP policy change that means officers are no longer required to wear name tags on their uniforms while on duty poses a threat to police accountability and transparency.
Officers now have option to wear name tag or 5-digit regimental number to identify themselves

Under a policy shift first reported by the Globe and Mail earlier this month, members of Canada's national police force can now choose between wearing a traditional name tag or their five-digit regimental number. The report said the policy has been in effect since March 30.

But defence lawyer Asaf Rashid said in an interview with CBC Radio's Information Morning Nova Scotia that officers should be required to display both, arguing that replacing names with numbers creates a barrier for the public during rapidly evolving situations.
“Who's going to be able to remember a number in a fast-paced environment where police are moving around very quickly,” Rashid said, describing the policy shift as a step toward "draconian" practices.

“There’s a certain sense of impunity when you don’t have your name tag on that maybe you can get away with it. They should be accountable, they should be transparent, and there shouldn’t be any limit on that.”

Rashid represented several people who were charged when a large group of protesters clashed with Halifax Regional Police more than five years ago during the controversial homeless encampment evictions in the city's downtown.
“In one particular case there was an officer who said he forgot to bring the uniform that had his name tag on it and he seemed to be taking certain liberties away from individuals," Rashid said.

The RCMP introduced the policy change to protect officers from online harassment and "doxing," the compilation and release of someone's personal information, including their name, address and phone number.
“Officers were targeted online and their private life was exposed based on their last name,” RCMP spokesperson Sgt. Maj. Julie Gagnon said.
In some cases, Gagnon said, officers received death threats.
“We sure don't want that for officers. So we're now giving the options … because the name might be just easier to find on open sources online,” she said.

Gagnon said a regimental number is unique to each officer and is just as effective as a surname for identification. She maintained that members of the public can still submit complaints or identify officers by providing either their name or regimental number to a local detachment.
“The public does not have to worry about the accountability of the RCMP because we are accountable for our actions and we will remain accountable for our actions,” Gagnon said.
However, the change reopens a debate highlighted in a 2024 report by the Civilian Review and Complaints Commission for the RCMP.

The oversight body looked into an incident where officers removed their name tags during a protest in British Columbia. It determined the practice was unreasonable without an alternative form of identification.
“It is much harder to hold the police accountable for their actions,” the report said. “This eats away at the public’s trust in the police.”
While the RCMP decided to permit regimental numbers in place of name tags during protests, the commission found that numbers were still difficult for the public to remember in high-stress situations.
Instead, the commission recommended officers wear "prominent but simple codes on the front and back of their uniforms" during public demonstrations.

articles.title: Oktoberfest opens as Munich mayor taps first beer keg
articles.summary: Thousands of visitors streamed onto Munich's Oktoberfest grounds as the world-famous beer festival got underway. Some spent the night outside the gates to secure coveted places in the festival tents.

image.caption: The ceremonial keg tapping at the Schottenhamel tent officially marks the start of Munich's Oktoberfest, which runs until October 4Image: Sven Hoppe/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The 191st Munich Oktoberfest officially opened at noon on Saturday, with the city's new mayor tapping the festival's first barrel of beer.
The annual ceremony, which takes place at midday, is always an eagerly awaited event, with no beer served until it has taken place.
Relief for Munich's new mayor

Green Party politician Dominik Krause needed just two strikes of the mallet for his first ceremonial tapping before handing the first liter mug of beer to Bavarian Premier Markus Söder of the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU).

Krause had practiced for the occasion with a personal tapping coach. The 36-year-old had said he hoped to open the barrel with two or three strikes. His predecessor, Dieter Reiter of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), had set a high standard by regularly opening the first barrel with two strikes.

After the tapping, Krause then presented the first liter of beer to Bavarian Premier Markus Söder of the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU). It's the first time Söder has received the ceremonial drink from a Green mayor.
Cannon fire then signalled that beer may be served throughout the festival grounds.
Oktoberfest: What to know about 'the best party in Germany'
Revelers race to grab drinking spots
Crowds had earlier rushed onto the Oktoberfest grounds in the southern German city of Munich shortly after the gates opened at 9 a.m on Saturday.

Some visitors ran toward the beer tents to claim the best seats after waiting for several hours. Members of the first group in line said they had arrived at 7 p.m. on Friday with camping chairs, sleeping bags and emergency blankets.
Organizers briefly held back sections of the crowd at the entrance, allowing people onto the grounds in stages and preventing a more concentrated rush.
How big is Oktoberfest?
More than 6 million people are expected to attend the 191st Oktoberfest, which runs for 16 days until October 4.
The festival, known locally as the Wiesn, features beer tents, fairground rides, traditional Bavarian food and live music.
Opening day was expected to bring blue skies and temperatures of up to 24 degrees Celsius (75 degrees Fahrenheit).
How much is an Oktoberfest beer?
A 1-liter (1.8-pint) beer costs between €14.80 and €15.90 ($17–$18.27) this year.
The average price has risen by 2.38% compared with last year to €15.61.

An analysis found that the average price has almost quintupled since 1985, when a liter of beer cost about 6.25 deutschmarks — equivalent to €3.20 at the fixed conversion rate. Consumer prices have risen by about 120% over the same period.

articles.title: US court rejects Trump policy on third-country deportations
articles.summary: The Trump administration has deported more than 25,000 people to countries other than their own. Now a federal appeals court has put the brakes on the policy.

image.caption: The second Trump administration has sent more than 25,000 migrants to 3rd countries [FILE: August 27, 2026]Image: Ketlain Difficile/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: A US federal appeals court has largely upheld a ruling blocking the Trump administration from rapidly deporting migrants to third countries without giving them a meaningful chance to raise safety concerns.

The three-judge panel of the US Court of Appeals for the First Circuit in Boston said Friday that migrants must receive effective notice of their intended destination and an opportunity to challenge removal if they fear persecution or torture there.
What did the court say about the DHS policy?

The case challenges a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) policy allowing migrants with final deportation orders to be sent to countries other than their own, provided authorities have diplomatic assurances they will not face persecution or torture.
The court said the policy could deny protections to migrants sent to unfamiliar countries without notice.
The Trump administration is expected to appeal the ruling to the Supreme Court.
DHS General Counsel James Percival said on X that the policy remains in force because Friday's ruling has not yet taken effect.
"If you claim fear in your home country, DHS has the right to send you elsewhere," Percival wrote.

The order comes as two men deported by the US to Equatorial Guinea were arbitrarily detained, with police covering their heads with bags, beating them and holding them at gunpoint in a hotel turned into a detention center, the AP reported.
More than 25,000 deported to third countries

Since US President Donald Trump returned to office, his administration has sent more than 25,000 migrants to at least 29 third countries, according to Third Country Deportation Watch, a project run by Refugees International and Human Rights First.
Some of the third countries immigrants are being deported to are:

items: South Sudan
Eswatini
Uganda
Equatorial Guinea
Liberia
Central African Republic

blocks.text: The third-country deals have drawn criticism from human rights groups, as several participating nations have notoriously repressive governments and poor human rights records.

articles.title: What commuters can do to protect themselves from haze
articles.summary: The Department of Health (DOH) on Saturday urged the public, particularly those who spend long hours on the road, to take precautions amid the health risks posed by haze.

blocks.text: Published September 19, 2026 4:31pm
The Department of Health (DOH) on Saturday urged the public, particularly those who spend long hours on the road, to take precautions amid the health risks posed by haze.

Citing a report from the Office of Civil Defense, the DOH said areas under close air quality monitoring include Negros Occidental, Negros Oriental, Siquijor, Cebu, Bohol, and all provinces in Mindanao.
To protect themselves from the effects of haze, the DOH urged the public to:

items: Wear an N95 mask. Alternatively, use a damp handkerchief or cloth to cover the mouth and nose, or wear a double surgical mask.
Wash the eyes with clean water or saline solution, and avoid rubbing them while outdoors.
Drink plenty of water to help flush irritants from the throat.
Take time to rest in enclosed spaces away from road smoke and dust.

blocks.text: The DOH also advised the public to call the national emergency hotline 911 or local emergency hotlines if they need assistance.
“Paalala para sa mga pampublikong drayber, delivery riders, street vendors, at field workers na madalas nasa kalsada, sundin ang mga gabay at paalala mula sa DOH ngayong may haze,” the DOH said.
(Reminders for public utility drivers, delivery riders, street vendors, and field workers who are often on the road: follow the guidelines and reminders from the DOH while haze is present.)
“Tandaan, laging unahing protektahan ang iyong kalusugan!” it added.
(Remember, always prioritize protecting your health!)
The DOH said the observed haze is likely smoke and transboundary haze from forest fires in Kalimantan, Indonesia, carried into the country by the Southwest Monsoon (Habagat). —VBL, GMA News

articles.title: LTO suspends licenses of 2 drivers for obstructing firetrucks in Makati
articles.summary: The Land Transportation Office (LTO) has suspended the licenses of two drivers caught in viral videos disrupting separate firetruck responses in Makati City.

blocks.text: Published September 19, 2026 4:30pm
The Land Transportation Office (LTO) has suspended the licenses of two drivers caught in viral videos disrupting separate firetruck responses in Makati City.

Announcing the development in a press release issued Saturday, the LTO released its findings for each case following hearings conducted by its Intelligence and Investigation Division (IID), pursuant to show-cause orders issued to the two motorists.

In one viral video, a driver was caught double-parking along Macabulos St. in Barangay Bangkal. The driver admitted to double-parking, explaining that his vehicle was under repair and could not be moved at the time.

"Inamin ng drayber na nakaparada ang kanyang sasakyan at nakaharang sa daanan, bagama't ipinaliwanag niyang inaayos noon ang sasakyan, nakapatong ito sa jack at natanggal ang isang gulong kaya hindi agad mailipat," LTO said.

(The driver admitted that his vehicle was parked and blocking the road, though he explained that it was being repaired at the time—mounted on a jack with one wheel removed—making it impossible to move immediately.)

The driver was found guilty of traffic obstruction and parking in prohibited specified places. He was also declared an improper person to operate a motor vehicle, resulting in a three-month suspension of his driver's license.
Meanwhile, the second incident in Guadalupe Nuevo showed a driver seemingly refusing to make way for a responding firetruck approaching from behind.
The driver claimed he had no intention of obstructing the firetruck and simply could not find a spot to pull over. However, LTO said footage showed otherwise.
"Gayunman, makikita sa video na may mga espasyo sa kanang bahagi ng kalsada kung saan maaari sanang pansamantalang tumabi ang drayber upang bigyang-daan ang rumerespondeng fire truck," the LTO said.
(However, the video clearly shows available space on the right side of the road where the driver could have temporarily pulled over to make way for the responding fire truck.)

The driver was found guilty of violating failure to yield right of way for police and other emergency vehicles and obstruction of traffic. He was likewise declared an improper person to operate a motor vehicle, resulting in a one-year suspension of his driver's license.
The driver's licenses of both individuals have been surrendered to the IID, while their vehicles remain under alarm status.
LTO chief Assistant Secretary Markus Lacanilao urged the public to strictly follow traffic laws and reminded motorists to always give way to emergency vehicles.

"Paalala natin sa mga motorista na laging bigyang-daan ang mga emergency vehicle, lalo na ang mga fire truck na rumeresponde. Bawat segundo ay mahalaga dahil may mga buhay na maaaring nakasalalay sa bawat pagresponde,” Lacanilao said.
(May we remind motorists to always give way to emergency vehicles, especially responding fire trucks. Every second counts because lives may be at stake during every response.)
— VDV, GMA News

articles.title: LIST: Community events, activities on 54th Martial Law commemoration
articles.summary: From card games and pop culture trivia to film screenings and other activities, here are engaging ways to reflect and honor history this Martial Law anniversary

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Filipinos will mark the 54th anniversary of Martial Law on September 21, 2026, commemorating the declaration of Proclamation No. 1081 by then-president Ferdinand E. Marcos. It ushered in a dark period in Philippine history, marked by widespread human rights abuses and a crackdown on free speech.

While street protests remain a central fixture of remembrance, several groups are set to organize educational forums, film screenings, art exhibits, and interactive community gatherings across the country.
Here is a running list you can check to participate in this year’s Martial Law Anniversary:
Outside Metro Manila
The ninth installment of the 1081 exhibit, honoring the victims of Ferdinand Marcos’ dictatorship, is open to visitors until Monday, September 21, at the UP Cebu Performing Arts Hall.

Students from UP Baguio will conduct alternative educational sessions in commemoration of the anniversary. Baguio-Benguet Laban sa Korapsyon will host talks, forums, and film viewings throughout the week, leading up to an assembly at the university on Monday, September 21, at 5:30 pm.

The UP Los Baños College of Arts and Sciences will screen seven short films about the Martial Law period at the CAS Auditorium on Monday, September 21, at 4 pm. Admission is free with online registration.
On Monday, September 21, at 6 pm EDT (720 Spadina Ave, Canada), Anakbayan Toronto will host an educational discussion on historical resistance, anti-fascism, and organizing.
Metro Manila

DIKTADOR! is an immersive role-playing card game about Martial Law history and Filipino resistance organized by Project Gunita. The creators are partnering with different organizations to hold game nights throughout the month:

items: Project Gunita: Saturday, September 19, 9 am, at the Constantino Foundation
DLSU University Student Government: Thursday to Friday, September 24 to 25, 4:15 pm at the Exhibit Area, Henry Sy Sr. Hall. Interested participants can register online.
UP Diliman CSWCD: Friday, September 25, 4 pm, at Bulwagang Tandang Sora (Registration details on their page)

blocks.text: The Women’s Legal and Human Rights Bureau Inc. is organizing a trivia night about Martial Law history and current events on Sunday, September 20, 12 pm, at Sunshineboy Cafe in Mahinhin 57, Quezon City. The event will also feature Project Gunita’s DIKTADOR! card game. Register for free (solo or as a team) online.
View this post on Instagram A post shared by Sunshineboy Cafe (@sunshineboyph)

GABRIELA Youth UP Manila and AlterMidya are hosting a screening of Igpaw Pasulong, which highlights stories of the Filipino masses during Martial Law. The event takes place at the UP Manila Theater on Wednesday, September 23, at 1 pm, followed by a discussion with women activists linking these narratives to present struggles. Registration fee is P30.

The DLSU Committee on National Issues and Concerns (CoNIC), in partnership with Active Vista, is screening Aswang on Thursday, September 24, 2:30 pm, at the Teresa Yuchengco Auditorium. The 2019 documentary investigates extrajudicial killings during the war on drugs. Online registration is required.

articles.title: After 20 years with no police force, safety tops voter concerns in this Quebec community
articles.summary: Provincial election signs are up in Chief Steeve Mathias’s community of Long Point First Nation, but he says there’s been silence when it comes to the issue he wants heard for his community of 600…

image.caption: Chief of Long Point First Nation Steeve Mathias is speaking out about the need for the return of the community's police force. Ahead of the upcoming provincial election, he says he wants 'to see a government that cares.' (Ismaël Houdassine/Radio-Canada)

blocks.text: Montreal

Provincial election signs are up in Chief Steeve Mathias’s community of Long Point First Nation, but he says there’s been silence when it comes to the issue he wants heard for his community of 600 people in Quebec’s Abitibi-Témiscamingue region.
‘It’s a human right to have public security,’ says Long Point First Nation chief

Provincial election signs are up in Chief Steeve Mathias’s community of Long Point First Nation, but he says there’s been silence when it comes to the issue he wants addressed for his community: an independent police force.
The community of 600, located in Winneway, Que., 630 kilometres northwest of Montreal in the Abitibi-Témiscamingue region, has been waiting to get their own police service reinstated for 20 years.

In the meantime, they’ve had to come up with their own solutions while relying on the closest available provincial police station in Ville-Marie, Que., 100 kilometres away — where Mathias says officers can take two to three hours to arrive in an emergency.
“We're trying to take all the different types of measures … through our own means that are very limited," Mathias said.

The long-term impact of the policing desert is contributing to an increase in violence and drugs, he says. He argues the problem wouldn’t be this serious if the community had a consistent police presence.
“We're getting a lot of pressure from our people. They say, ‘do something about the drug dealing … it's getting out of hand, completely out of control,’” he said.
Ahead of the Oct. 5 provincial election, Mathias is speaking out, noting he wants “to see a government that cares.”
“It’s a human right to have public security … and [it] seems like my community is not eligible,” he said.
‘I feel safer now with my door locked,’ says resident
The police force in Winneway was officially dismantled on March 31, 2006, when a tripartite agreement with the federal and provincial governments ended.
A number of issues led to it, including a failure to come to an agreement on matters such as a lack of resources, infrastructure, jurisdiction and the number of police officers, says Mathias.
The band council began incurring a deficit, he says — significant and untenable for a community of its size.
After the police force was dismantled, the provincial police took charge. Over the years, Mathias says they stopped patrolling regularly.

items: Indigenous turnout remains low in Quebec amid calls for political inclusion

blocks.text: Now, the response time can be lengthy and is contributing to heightened fear.
“I never used to lock my door at night,” said resident Diane Polson. “I feel safer now with my door locked.”
A lifelong resident of Winneway and interim director of the child-care centre, Polson says the question of security and safety is top of mind for her.
Twenty years ago, Polson served as part of a negotiating team in an effort to keep and expand the small police force the community had in the early 2000s.
In 2022, the community signed a collaboration agreement with the province for a temporary police force made up of officers from neighbouring First Nations.

items: After years of demands, this Quebec First Nation will finally get its own police force
First Nation issues state of emergency amid growing violence, asks Quebec police to step up

blocks.text: But Mathias notes one of its conditions stipulated that provincial police still needed to be present for interventions.
“The two First Nation police services cannot come to the community without … the Sûreté du Québec being present,” he said.
“People found that very ridiculous. You know, there was a situation happening in the community and then like our First Nation police, they couldn't intervene.”
The office of Quebec's minister responsible for relations with First Nations and Inuit, Ian Lafrenière, said the situation involves complex challenges that predate its government.
He agreed that the area should have police coverage, but said the government would not negotiate publicly.
Training locals to protect community
For now, the community is mobilizing to find solutions. It's hired a private security firm to train about 15 to 18 locals to help keep residents safe.
With the plan to purchase a vehicle for security agents to patrol the community, Mathias says the community is trying to give a sense of security particularly to elders, women and youth.

Last winter — in response to growing concerns from residents over the presence of drugs and violence in town — the Long Point First Nation held a general assembly where a decision was made to mandate the council to take action. It allowed them to forbid certain individuals from coming into the community.
LISTEN | Chief Mathias calls on candidates to bring back police force:
Quebec AM11:20Long Point First Nation calls on provincial candidates to bring back police force
As part of this resolution, an individual who lives outside the community was banned. Mathias says he's known in the community as a drug dealer.
But the chief notes, without resources to enforce such bans, there are concerns about violence escalating.
“I find that very shameful that the government are not taking these matters more seriously [as] they should,” he said.
“Take accountability… provide the means and the resources.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Rachel Watts is a journalist with CBC News in Quebec City. Originally from Montreal, she enjoys covering stories in the province of Quebec. You can reach her at rachel.watts@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Were mosquitos bugging you more than usual this summer? Blame the rain
articles.summary: If it felt like mosquitoes were been particularly bad this summer — and hanging around for longer — it might not be in your head.

image.caption: Wet weather brought swarms of mosquitoes to parts of Canada this summer, while a major storm that hit southern Ontario earlier this month has led to the pests sticking around for longer. (Corlaffra/Shutterstock)

blocks.text: Canada·New
If it felt like mosquitoes were been particularly bad this summer — and hanging around for longer — it might not be in your head.
Parts of Canada had particularly bad mosquito season, with critters sticking around longer in southern Ontario
Some prairie cities saw a mosquito population boom earlier this summer, with some stores in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta running out of bug spray entirely due to high demand.
Data collected by the City of Edmonton showed the number of mosquitoes in the city was 15 times higher in July compared to the same time last year.

"While these do not represent record high mosquito numbers for our region, they are a stark contrast to the previous two summer seasons, which can magnify public perception," said Peter Daly, a biological sciences technologist at the City of Edmonton.
Saskatoon and Winnipeg also saw higher numbers of mosquitoes in July compared to last year, according to data from those cities.
In southern Ontario, experts say the record rainfall parts of the region saw this summer is likely to blame for the mosquito boom, and why they're still causing itchy red welts well into September.

Fiona Hunter, a medical and veterinary entomology professor at Brock University, said this summer, southern Ontario has seen greater numbers of the Ochlerotatus trivittatus species compared to other years.

Ochlerotatus trivittatus is known as a floodwater mosquito that lays its eggs in low-lying areas filled with water, so the amount of rain southern Ontario has seen this year has created ideal conditions for them, she said.
"Think about all the rain we've had in southern Ontario this year. Soggy fields, low spots in lawns, roadside depressions and other poorly drained areas have repeatedly filled with water," she said.
"That creates lots of potential habitat for this particular mosquito, and probably helps explain why we're seeing so many of them this year."

items: Seeing more mosquitoes than normal this time of year? You're not alone
'Skeeter syndrome' showing up in Alberta as mosquito populations boom

blocks.text: The species is known to be a very persistent biter, she said.
"So I suspect people are simply coming into contact with this species more often this year, which may be part of the reason mosquitoes seem especially bad right now."

The torrential downpour that pummelled the Greater Toronto Area and many other communities across southern and southwestern Ontario also may have triggered the hatching of a whole bunch of dormant mosquito eggs, said Rosalind Murray, an assistant professor of biology at the University of Toronto.
"And so we might see a little bit of a blip where we have a bit of a boom, especially in places that have major flood flooding like Toronto," she told CBC Radio's Metro Morning.
Mosquito season stretches into September after wet summer in Ottawa
Colder temps will drive populations down
But as soon as the region starts to see colder overnight temperatures, the mosquitoes won't be an issue anymore.
"They don't do very well when it's extremely hot, they can dry out. They also are going to die immediately once it gets cold," Murray said.
"Once we start seeing those really cool nighttime temperatures, like below 10 C, we should start to see them peter out. And as soon as we have a frost, they'll be gone."
That's what Alberta has seen happen after a recent cold snap, said Ken Fry, an entomology instructor at Olds College in Olds, Alta.
Edmonton and Calgary experienced a particularly bad mosquito season earlier this summer, driven by a large amount of rainfall early on in the year.
But then, he said, mosquito populations "pretty much crashed" due to colder temperatures in recent weeks.

items: Edmonton has 15 times more mosquitoes now than at same time last year, city scientist says

blocks.text: Daly said Edmonton has already seen numbers drop for the most dominant local mosquito species, Aedes vexans, but added that since the city has had a warm fall so far, "we’ve yet to see quite as precipitous drop in their numbers as some other years. "
Fry said the critters might make a reappearance as temperatures are expected to climb back to 20 C or higher over the next week in the region.
"But we won't have the populations, I don't think, anywhere near close to what central Canada is experiencing."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Sarah Petz is a Toronto-based senior writer with the CBC News live pages team. Born and raised in Manitoba, her career has taken her across three provinces, multiple cities and to northern Uganda.

articles.title: Professional cyclists can top 100 km/h. But safety has not kept pace — and people are dying
articles.summary: As the world’s top cyclists descend upon Montreal, there’s a spectre looming over the event: at least 11 of their compatriots have died in professional races and training rides this year, adding to a…

image.caption: Riders emerge from yellow smoke for the final kilometres of the 2nd stage of the 113th Tour de France on July 5 in Barcelona. At least 11 cyclists have died in professional events and training races this year, prompting a call for better safety measures. (Anne-Christine Poujoulat/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: As the world's top cyclists descend upon Montreal for the UCI Road World Championships, there's a spectre looming over the event.
At least 11 of their compatriots have died in professional races and training rides this year, adding to a growing tally of injuries and deaths in the elite sport.
Though safety gear is being developed alongside the evolution of bicycles that can move faster than ever before, an underlying conflict remains in the sport: at what point must safety trump speed?

Right now, the average speed of the Tour de France winner is 43.3 km/h, set in 2026 — exactly 19 km/h faster than the average speed set by the winner 100 years ago. On the descents, riders now reach upwards of 100 km/h.

Safety technology that might slow riders down, such as wider handlebars, are being considered by the governing body, Union Cycliste Internationale (UCI), and SafeR, an international safety taskforce. Other measures being floated include choosing safer courses, tracking riders in real-time and adopting protective equipment like airbags.
But it has divided riders, some of whom argue that slowing bikes down goes against the spirit of professional cycling — and even those within SafeR, like Adam Hansen, have doubts.

"It's hard to get my head around this, because that's the whole purpose of the sport, is to go as fast as possible," said Hansen, a former professional Australian cyclist and current president of the pro cyclists' union.
Others, like Canada's Michael Woods — who estimates he has endured between 30 and 40 crashes — says changes are critical to prevent future fatalities.

"The bike that I'm on now versus the bike that I first started racing on [in 2010] is night and day," said Woods, whose professional racing career took him across Europe, including winning a stage of the 2023 Tour de France.
"The speeds that you can hit are far higher. But the rules … haven't caught up and that's made the sport far more dangerous."
GPS trackers

Woods and Hansen believe that GPS trackers, which will be used in Montreal, should be mandatory in all races. The trackers will sit underneath the bike's saddle and can transmit real-time data to a central location so that rescuers can respond immediately in the case of a crash.

Earlier this month, against the backdrop of the Aug. 14 death of 19-year-old British rider Finlay Tarling at the Volta race in Portugal, UCI "stressed the urgent need to put in place, as quickly as possible, a dedicated safety system allowing the real-time location of riders and vehicles to be tracked at all professional road cycling events."
The statement also noted that "in discussions on safety, stakeholders need to move past any disagreements on certain issues and act together."
Muriel Furrer's legacy
GPS trackers for pro cycling were introduced at the UCI Road World Championships in Rwanda last year following the death of Muriel Furrer.

The 18-year-old Swiss cyclist lay critically injured for an hour and 20 minutes after she careened off the wet, leaf-strewn road into a secluded wooded area during the 2024 championships in Zurich. She was airlifted to hospital and later died.

items: Swiss teenage cyclist Muriel Furrer dies after crashing at road world championships

blocks.text: Woods, who was at that competition, recalls how the race continued even after Furrer's death.
" The sport's wild in that sense," he said. "When a rider passes away, it's sad. Everyone's impacted by it, but they didn't cancel the event.

"It's the same with other incidents ... where I've raced where professional riders have died [where] maybe we took things a bit easier the next day, or had a moment of silence — but the race continued."

Woods retired from professional cycling last year, because he no longer felt he could race safely. In March 2020, he broke his right femur during the Paris-Nice race. Last year, he woke up in an ambulance with a broken collarbone and a severe concussion after crashing out at the Milano-Torino race.
He's decided, however, to race one last time at the Road World Championships this week so he can end his career in Canada instead of abroad.
Airbags
While GPS trackers can ensure riders will get faster medical attention following a crash, they don't prevent injury itself. Airbags, meanwhile, might help.
In January, UCI put out a call for airbags that could be part of a bike frame and for those that could integrate into a cyclist's clothing.

items: Canadian cyclist calls for improved rider safety after latest crash-riddled start to Tour de France

blocks.text: The latter can be part of bike pants, said Hansen, and has straps around the shoulders.

"When it goes off, it actually puts a ring around your neck area, and it actually covers your collarbone," he said. "It really protects your spine, protects your neck ... [and] goes almost up to your helmet."
Several prototypes are in development, he said. The challenge in the past has been creating something light enough that it won't hinder a rider's speed or their movement.

At least two World Tour teams (Picnic PostNL and Visma-Lease a Bike) are testing out the Aerobag, according to Cycling News. It's not yet on the market nor has it been approved for UCI races; it's unclear exactly when such a measure might be adopted.
Other sports have adopted similar airbags, both in downhill skiing and recreational motorcyclists.
Top Ottawa cyclist Michael Woods announces retirement
Bike lanes can be dangerous for the pros
Speed isn't the only factor in these crashes.

Woods says UCI has been studying the design of cycling courses, and found that the same elements that make recreational cyclists safer — such as bike lanes with bollards, speed bumps or roundabouts — can be hazardous in a race.
Canadian cyclist Alex Volstad says that when she's in a tight group of riders, known as a peloton, she has limited visibility and may be slower to react.
"Sometimes if it hits you by surprise, then you can get a bit, like, bucked off your bike, like you're riding a horse," she said.
In 2026, for example, a bottleneck of riders approaching a roundabout in the Tour of Oman created a major pileup before the final sprint, knocking some off their bikes.

It's one of the reasons race organizers often favour rural areas, like Saint-Georges, Que., where nationals were held this year, because there's less infrastructure on the road to endanger competitors.
Sometimes, though, it's the simple things that can make a difference, says Michael Barry, a retired professional road racer — like your eyesight.
Just a simple eye test would make a fairly big difference.- Michael Barry, retired cycling racer
Early in his career, he raced without his glasses, because he had a light prescription and the rain, dirt and other debris that could collect on the lenses might slow him down or worsen visibility.
Then, he missed some gravel when he was flying down the French Alps in the ‘90s. He broke his femur in the ensuing crash.
After that, he got custom racing glasses. Soon, some of his teammates did the same, which was uncommon at the time.
It's why he thinks riders should have to get their eyes tested. With riders going as fast as cars, he said it's critical that they have perfect eyesight.
"They're testing for every other physical attribute the riders have," he said. "So just a simple eye test would make a fairly big difference."

articles.title: Russian drones are stalking Ukrainian trains and trying to hobble the country's rail system
articles.summary: In recent weeks, Russia has stepped up drone strikes on Ukraine's rail network, targeting trains and the approximately 20,000 kilometres of track that form a key transportation artery across the…

image.caption: A woman looks out the window of Ukrainian passenger rail car in Lviv, Ukraine, on Thursday. (Angela Johnston/CBC)

blocks.text: World·New

In recent weeks, Russia has stepped up drone strikes on Ukraine's rail network, targeting trains and the approximately 20,000 kilometres of track that form a key transportation artery across the country.
At least 1 person was killed and 7 were injured after the latest strike on a train in the Kharkiv region

When railworkers aboard a train travelling between the Ukrainian cities of Odesa and Dnipro began shouting at passengers to evacuate the carriages early Thursday, Anastasia Rybalchenko's mind immediately began racing through worst-case scenarios.
It was 4 a.m., an air-raid alert was in effect, and Russian drones had already struck a number of Ukrainian trains that week, including one just a few kilometres from the Polish border.

Rybalchenko, 17, and other sleepy passengers exited the train and trudged through the grass in a rural area that was about a 15-minute ride from her final destination, Kropyvnytskyi. When she was about 200 to 300 metres from the tracks, she put down a blanket and sat on the ground.

Rybalchenko drifted in and out of sleep while waiting for the all-clear to return to the train. But about two hours later, she was abruptly jolted awake by the sound of something whooshing overhead, followed by a series of explosions.
"We started running into the bushes and hiding," she said in a phone interview with CBC News from her home in Kropyvnytskyi.
"My heart was pounding like crazy. I didn't understand what was happening or what to do."
She quickly learned that it wasn't her train that was on fire, but infrastructure along the railway line.
Inside one of Russia’s key targets in its war on Ukraine
One of Russia's key targets
In recent weeks, Russia has stepped up strikes on Ukraine's rail network, targeting trains and the approximately 20,000 kilometres of track that form a key transportation artery across the country.

With Ukrainian airspace closed, the rail network carries passengers across the country, and in some cases, across the border into Poland. With shipping in the Black Sea under constant threat, the rail network is also a key corridor for supplies and goods, including grain and aid.

items: Russian drones hit bus, train in Ukraine, killing 5: officials
Ukraine has been trying to bring the war to Russia. More Russians are beginning to feel it

blocks.text: Earlier in the war, Ukrainian Railways frequently highlighted its ability to keep most trains running on schedule despite Russia's full-scale invasion. Now, the network is facing multi-hour delays, while new rules approved by the government Thursday prohibit passengers from boarding or disembarking during a red alert, which indicates a threat of a missile attack.

Russia's Foreign Ministry insists that railway hubs serving Ukraine's military are legitimate targets, while other Russian officials specifically claim that the attacks are on infrastructure related to the shipment of military cargo from Europe.
But Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says the deadly attacks are part of the Kremlin's strategy to destroy the country's economy and disrupt daily life.
Mounting risk
This year, two dozen railway workers have been killed and more than 80 injured.

On Friday morning, at least one person was killed and seven others injured when a drone struck a train in the Kharkiv region. Officials with Ukrainian Railways said some of those injured were passengers who had not moved far enough away from the train during the evacuation.
In a statement, the rail operator said people need to stay 200 metres away from trains and railway infrastructure.
Russia attacks commuter train in Ukraine's Kharkiv region

Russia has intensified its attacks on Ukraine's rail network by launching jet-powered drones, which can travel at speeds of up to 600 kilometres per hour and carry heavier payloads than earlier models.
Ukrainian officials say Russia is mass-producing the drones, churning out as many as 3,000 a month and that the drones' speed makes them more difficult to intercept.
Earlier this week, Zelenskyy chaired a meeting that looked at how to bolster the protection of the country's railway network, and also replenish its stock of damaged cars.
Officials say around 300 locomotives and 120 passenger carriages were struck so far this year.

items: Zelenskyy describes Canada-U.S. tensions as 'strange,' draws comparison to Ukraine and Russia

blocks.text: Drone attack close to Polish border
It was a jet-powered drone that struck a locomotive on Sunday while the train was parked a few kilometres from the Polish border.
Shortly before that strike, a train carrying former British prime minister Boris Johnson and other diplomats travelled through the same area before crossing into Poland.
Western Ukraine is typically far removed from the bulk of Russian strikes. But this week, Poland was forced to close two of its airports several times because of Russian drones near its borders.
Yulia Zaletska, 40, a train steward who has worked on Ukrainian trains since 2017, described heightened tension among railway staff and passengers.
"There are a lot of emotions, but you have to control yourself, because we are responsible for a large number of people," she told CBC News while working aboard a train travelling from Lviv to Kyiv.

She said she now frequently gets stress headaches before taking what she considers more dangerous routes in the eastern part of the country. On one journey to Dnipro, she said she had to evacuate passengers five separate times.
Sleepless nights, and stressful days

Conductor Andrii Hul' explained that a team at Ukrainian Railways monitors ongoing threats and, when necessary, makes the decision to stop a train. Information is then communicated to the conductor, who must also help determine where it is safe to stop.
Hul' considers himself lucky as he has not yet had to carry out an evacuation, but the 20-year veteran of Ukraine's railways says the intensifying attacks are taking a toll.
He frequently spends nights sleeping in a shelter during air raids, only to get up in the morning and drive a train.

"What would we do without the railway?" he said. "I would say it would be very difficult for people to get through this, because there are places where the railway is the only means of transport available to people."
For Rybalchenko, still shaken by Thursday's evacuation and the explosions, she says she will stick to travelling by car or bus in the future.
"It was really frightening … and after this trip, I'm not planning to travel by train anymore," she said.
"At least you'll get there, and you won't be delayed for five or six hours somewhere, and there won't be an evacuation."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Briar Stewart is a CBC correspondent, based in London. During her nearly two decades with CBC, she has reported across Canada and internationally. She can be reached at briar.stewart@cbc.ca or on X @briarstewart.

blocks.text: A last-minute logistics problem has cost shot-putter Tajinderpal Singh Toor his spot as India's male flagbearer at Saturday's Asian Games opening ceremony in Nagoya, Japan.
Kabaddi player Pawan Sehrawat is set to step in instead, joining shooter Manu Bhaker, a two-time Paris Olympics bronze medalist, who will be India's female flagbearer.
Toor, who is chasing a third consecutive Asian Games gold in shot put, said he only learned of his selection as flagbearer a day earlier and that his kit was still back in India.

"I'm told that my kit will reach at 3 p.m. at the airport. Reaching the opening ceremony venue after collecting my kit from the airport on time will be very difficult," he told news agency PTI, adding that he had informed the Indian Olympic Association (IOA) that he would not be attending the ceremony.
The Indian Olympic Association said in a statement that Toor would be unable to serve as flagbearer "due to a technical issue."
The mix-up was one of several hiccups in the run-up to the Games, which open on Saturday with more than 17,000 athletes competing across more than 40 sports through October 4.

Organizers, working without a traditional athletes' village, have housed competitors in container-style huts, hotels and a cruise ship. There have been complaints over accommodation quality, transport delays, and a mistaken playing of North Korea's national anthem for South Korea's men's hockey team.
A tropical storm bearing down on the region threatens to cause further disruption as competition gets underway.
