blocks.text: I found love at an Irish matchmaking festival - and I want others to do the same
"It was very serendipitous" - Mary and Jason on finding love in Ireland
BySheila Flynn
Senior US Reporter
Mary Timby was fed up with dating apps when she booked a trip to Ireland on a whim last summer - from the comfort of her Colorado couch.
The spur-of-the-moment trip was unlike her: Timby, 39, is a self-described "total planner".

But she'd always wanted to visit Ireland, and she found herself exhausted by the local dating scene while navigating a career transition. And then she remembered a few throwaway lines from a comedy series about a matchmaking festival in Ireland.
So she looked it up - and not only was the Lisdoonvarna Matchmaking Festival real, it was also taking place during the entire month of September, when she was scheduled to visit.

Now, a little more than a year later, Timby is reaping the benefits of that uncharacteristic last-minute decision: She's become a viral star. She's found love with an Irishman she met at a pub called The Matchmaker. And she's even started a new business venture - bringing others to Lisdoonvarna who hope to follow in her footsteps.
Image source, Mary Timby
Timby and Jason Mangan, 38, from County Clare, Ireland, are pursuing a transatlantic romance

"It's really about enjoying County Clare, enjoying the festival, and, if you meet someone, you do - and that's what happened with us," says Timby, smiling at her partner, Jason Mangan, sitting beside her.

They're speaking from the windswept coastal cottage they rented together for the summer in his native County Clare - about 20 miles (32 km) southwest of Lisdoonvarna, the site of their first fortuitous meeting.
'Mary, your video is going viral'
From the outset, Timby's inaugural Ireland trip seemed to take on a life of its own.

She filmed a short video on the plane before her flight took off, telling her approximately 300 TikTok followers that she was heading on an off-the-cuff trip to an Irish matchmaking festival - and didn't "know what's going to happen".
Timby then "turned my phone on airplane mode, then spent about eight hours on the flight (and) woke up at Shannon Airport," she says.
When she turned on her phone, "it was blowing up".
A group of friends had texted her. "They said, 'Mary, your video is going viral,'" she says. "I didn't even have notifications on for social media."
She rented a manual transmission car - horrified to find the gear stick on the left side of the driver's seat - and set off through County Clare to her accommodation at an Irish family's home.

Then she headed to Lisdoonvarna, where she saw firsthand that the festival is a whole-town, month-long celebration of conversation and dancing, rather than a line of singles waiting to be set up by a sage local matchmaker.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Colorado woman Mary Timby, 39, visited Ireland's Aran Islands with her new beau

blocks.text: Colorado woman Mary Timby, 39, visited Ireland's Aran Islands with her new beau

That's changed since the festival's origins 170 years ago, when bachelor farmers and moneyed visitors would flock to the spa town of Lisdoonvarna to bathe in its mineral-rich waters and socialise. Generations of matchmakers would ply their trade to set up successful marriages, and word spread. Now, while the town's year-round residents number fewer than 1,000, that number swells up to 80,000 each September as revellers descend upon Lisdoonvarna from around the world.

Third-generation matchmaker Willie Daly still holds court at his nearby home and at festival events, and Timby even visited him during her trip - when he put her on the phone to random men whose accents she struggled to understand.
But the real magic of contemporary Lisdoonvarna lies in the town's overflowing streets and pubs - as Timby soon found out.

Her first night in town was "a little slow," she admits - and Timby was tired and jet-lagged. She retired to her room and spent the next day sightseeing, but the Irish woman running her accommodation convinced her to try Lisdoonvarna again that night.
"My AirBnB host said, 'You should go back tonight, because I heard that the younger folks come out at night,'" laughs Timby.
So she did - and found herself dancing and drinking pints at The Matchmaker Bar in the centre of town. That's when a "handsome Irishman" approached her.
'Conversation just flowed'

"I went over and introduced myself, and... conversation just flowed," says Mangan, 38, from Ennis, County Clare, about 22 miles southeast of Lisdoonvarna. He'd been to the festival before and was well-acquainted with its cultural significance, remembering his grandparents making the journey decades earlier for the dancing.

"Unfortunately, I didn't have much time on my hands, because I was turning back to Ennis," says Mangan, designated driver that night for a group of friends. "So I got her name, and I said, 'Oh, sure, I might see you around.'
"It was a very short interaction, to be honest with you."

blocks.caption: Image caption, The couple first met at Lisdoonvarna's Matchmaker Bar during the annual festival

blocks.text: The couple first met at Lisdoonvarna's Matchmaker Bar during the annual festival
He didn't leave it at that, though; Mangan found Timby on Instagram and followed up with a message inviting her out.
"It was short and sweet, and it was really genuine, too," says Timby - and she took him up on the offer.

What followed was a series of whirlwind dates - lunches, dinners, sightseeing and shopping trips. Timby extended her time in Ireland and documented much of it for her newfound following - but she didn't reveal anything about her new beau. They wanted to save the burgeoning romance for themselves.
When Timby eventually had to fly home, there were "tears at the airport" - but they decided to keep the relationship going.
"It was very tough to say goodbye," Timby says. "It was very tough to start a long-distance relationship, but it ended up being a really good opportunity for us to sort of slow things down a bit."

They kept talking daily, Mangan impatiently waiting for Timby to wake up seven hours behind him in Colorado. She flew back to Ireland again, then he made his first trip to America for Thanksgiving 2025. Timby returned to Ireland at Christmas and met his family, and after that, they decided to make her boyfriend's big social media reveal.
"We thought, this is something we already know we want to invest in... we were ready to share," Timby says. "So New Year's Eve, we shared a photo of him, and people were just over-the-moon excited."

The pair watched their following grow, drawing interest from Irish cafes and tourist destinations to the local Gaelic sports club in Colorado. Their story also caught the attention of Lisdoonvarna locals, who approached Timby - a communications consultant - about being an ambassador for the festival.
"So I said: Sign me up," Timby laughs. "I love the festival. It brought me Jay."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Mangan has made repeated trips to Colorado since their 2025 meeting in Ireland

blocks.text: Mangan has made repeated trips to Colorado since their 2025 meeting in Ireland
Timby's been inundated with messages from lovelorn followers hoping to replicate her matchmaking success.

"I heard from many of my followers... groups of people wanting to go to the festival but not having anyone to go with" or "not knowing what to do," Timby says. "I really listened to that, and I also wanted to be mindful of the fact that I love Ireland.
"I'm so excited to showcase County Clare and all the amazing things that the west coast of Ireland has, but I'm also not a tour operator."

So she partnered with a company called Met Through Friends, which organises and encourages real-life meetups for people looking for love. They released an interest form for a trip, expecting "80 to 100 responses." They received 560.
The first group of eight will make the trip later this month, with Timby's Irish boyfriend consulting on the itinerary.

"You can go on all these apps, swipe left, swipe right, but it's not actually going out and making a connection with someone and experiencing a small little town in Ireland, experiencing the culture," says Mangan.
"It's a once-in-a-lifetime experience... you never know."
Timby, smiling at her boyfriend of one year, agrees.
"I echo everything Jay just said," she says. "Put your phone down and put yourselves out there, and good things will come."

articles.title: Tata Sons: India's corporate crown braces for upheaval amid boardroom revolt
articles.summary: The Tata boardroom battle has intensified over a re-appointment of its chairman and a diktat to go public.

blocks.text: This week, the board of Tata Sons - one of India's oldest conglomerates and owner of iconic British brands such as Jaguar Land Rover and Tetley Tea - defied its largest shareholder, Tata Trusts, by reappointing N Chandrasekaran as chairman and backing a public listing of the holding company.

Tata Trusts, which owns 66% of Tata Sons called the decision "illegal" under its articles of association and also opposed the listing, setting the stage for a period of prolonged upheaval and possibly a protracted legal drama at Bombay House, the headquarters of the 158-year-old company.
For the Tatas, who are no strangers to boardroom battles, a cloud of uncertainty now prevails at multiple levels.

The resolution to reappoint Chandrasekharan, while approved by the board, could be defeated at the company's Annual General Meeting as Tata Trusts is likely to vote against it, putting a question mark over his future.
The meeting has to take place before 31 December as per reports, after the previous one was adjourned for lack of quorum, but no new date has yet been announced.

"The Nomination and Remuneration Committee (NRC) of the Board of Tata Sons which reappointed him has no power to take this decision. They can only make a recommendation. Also, their decision flies against the governance code of the company that requires executives to step down from active roles at 65. These are serious lapses," Nitin Potdar, a prominent Mumbai-based corporate lawyer told the BBC.
Chandrasekharan, who got a five-year extension, will turn 65 in 2028.

Tata Group stocks first soared and then crashed as the tensions mounted, reflecting hope and uncertainty about leadership and business continuity amid several high-stakes but loss-making bets by Chandrasekharan in sectors like semiconductors and airlines.

But beyond the leadership tussle, the bigger question to contend with is the group's public listing, "which now looks increasingly inevitable", Nirmalya Kumar, who previously headed strategy at Tata Sons, told the BBC.

In 2022, India's central bank, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), classified Tata Sons as an "upper layer non-banking financial company" because of its systemic importance and investment activities. This created a listing obligation on the group.
Tata Sons sought to get out of this classification by repaying their debt and arguing that they do not borrow directly from the public markets.
But after sitting on its application for over two years, the RBI rejected the company's bid to get out of the framework earlier this month, pushing the group closer to a stock market debut.

In a statement, Tata Trusts reiterated its long-held opposition to going public and said "all available options and not a listing alone" are being explored even though its trustees are no longer unanimous in their position on the matter.
Potdar says the regulator has no power to force any company to go public and the issue will almost certainly be legally challenged by Tata Trusts.
The RBI meanwhile has pre-emptively, external approached the courts seeking to be heard first in any matter related to the ‌listing.
The issue has sharply divided opinion among corporate pundits.
Many in the group, including the late Ratan Tata and veteran director NA Soonawala, have long argued strongly for keeping the group private.
A publicly held Tata Sons could significantly reduce the control and special rights the Tata Trusts wield over the group.
They say the Tatas have a unique operating structure where the majority shareholder is a charity which uses dividends received from commercial arms to fund hospitals, universities and research.
A listing, they say, will destroy its character by making it accountable to outside shareholders whose focus would be financial returns.
"A new group of shareholders might say, 'Don't declare dividends; we need to reinvest this money in the companies.' What happens then? The first casualty will be the hospitals they run," said Potdar.

Opponents of the initial public offering (IPO) also worry that bringing in public investors will weaken the group's internal support function to rescue distressed businesses and expose the company to quarterly performance pressures.
Moreover the timing is another crucial factor.

"The group currently faces large financial commitments from recently formed subsidiary companies, including Air India, investments in long gestation projects, and losses in newer ventures," Soonawala wrote, external in a piece for Times of India.

"The current situation in the case of Air India would be an acid test. All these would need to be disclosed fully in an IPO prospectus. Consolidated financial statements – reflecting subsidiary losses and borrowings – may not present an especially attractive picture to sophisticated investors, pointing to wrong timing for an IPO at the present time."

Many, including Potdar, also argue that globally, industrial foundations are being protected as sources of patient capital - money that can be committed for years to fund long-gestation projects and social goals. By forcing the Tatas to list, India is going the other way.
But supporters of a listing say it would bring much-needed transparency and accountability to a group that is systemically important to India.

"There should be tougher scrutiny of their capital-allocation decisions being so central to the Indian business ecosystem. Everybody wants complete control over their empire and the freedom to take capricious decisions, but that is not a good thing for the organisation," said Kumar.

Collectively, listed Tata companies including Tata Motors and TCS have a market capitalisation of more than $260bn and influence over 17.7 million retail shareholders, pension funds, insurers and mutual funds, investment advisory firm InGovern said.
"[It] cannot reasonably remain outside the governance and transparency expectations increasingly associated with systemically important financial and industrial conglomerates," the report added.
It also argued that shareholders of listed Tata companies are indirectly affected by Tata Sons' decisions, even though they have no direct voting rights in the holding company.

Moreover, given that the Tatas have recently made several high stakes global bets, making iPhones for Apple, partnering with Nvidia on artificial intelligence and Boeing, Airbus and Singapore Airlines on aerospace and aviation, InGovern says, a "flexible and transparent capital structure increasingly important".
Some experts say a listing may now be the only way to ease increasingly fractious relations between the board and shareholders - tensions that are hurting not just the group, but India more broadly.
Tata Trusts hold controlling economic interest and veto rights over Tata Sons board appointments and capital allocation decisions above a certain threshold.

It's hard to imagine the latter can function effectively on crucial issues of national interest - such as turning around Air India or raising funds to pay off a large minority shareholder like the SP Group which is in urgent need of cash to avert a potentially ruinous default - if it can no longer see eye to eye with its biggest shareholder.
Whatever happens on the listing front, experts say India's biggest trophy asset is entering totally uncharted territory. As Kumar suspects, "a new twist" can be expected every week.
Follow BBC News India on Instagram, external, YouTube,, external X, external and Facebook, external.

articles.title: Grim discoveries of murdered women spark fear in South Africa
articles.summary: Dineo Motapane is one of nine recent victims whose deaths have left a nation traumatised over the level of violence against women.

blocks.text: "What we are going to do, I have no idea," sobs Nokwanda Matshikiza, reflecting on the murder of her niece Dineo Motapane. "But something must give."
"For us, for all the other women. How many other bodies will be found before something happens?"
Nokwanda is speaking to the BBC from the family home near South Africa's main city, Johannesburg, just two days after relatives identified Dineo's body.
The 38-year-old mother-of-two was last seen alive last Sunday. Her battered body, partly burned, found later in the residential region of Ekurhuleni.
Nokwanda weeps as she describes how the family will have to face, at some point, the grim task of telling Dineo's daughter of her death.
"How do you explain that your parent was brutally murdered, dumped in a field, and just left there, discarded like a piece of rubbish.
"There's no coming to peace with it," she adds. "It's something that you can never reconcile yourself with, that you can never get over."

Dineo's death this week has come amid a series of comparable incidents in Ekurhuleni – her body one of three discovered there this week. In total, nine bodies of murdered women have been found in similar circumstances in the region since July.

The problem has always been there but this spate of grim discoveries has once again sparked a national outcry about the scale of violence against women in the country – which has one of the highest rates of gender-based violence in the world.
Themba Kekana is also living in shock at the death of a loved one.
His sister, Itumeleng, was one of the first to disappear in Ekurhuleni.
The 32-year-old shopkeeper's body was found in July, 17 days after she was last seen alive. Her body was badly bruised, partially clothed and dumped on a bridge.
"We are devastated with grief," says Themba, wet eyes shining.
"I look at my sister's young daughter and my eyes fill with tears, I know there is no way that I can ever take this pain away from her.
"No family should have to deal with what we are faced with."
Only one arrest has been made in connection with the murders – and that was two days after the first body was discovered on 15 July.
Nobody has been detained following the murders of Itumeleng or Dineo or the other six Ekurhuleni women.
Most of the victims were young, in their 20s or 30s, and almost all had suffered extreme violence before their deaths.
Police have said they are not sure if they are hunting a serial killer. It is possible the cases are not linked.
Either way, what has happened in this residential district east of South Africa's biggest city has traumatised the nation, shining a spotlight on a situation that many believe is a crisis.
South Africa's police issue detailed crime statistics every quarter, which show that during the last quarter – between April and June this year - 5,427 people were murdered.

The official data does not distinguish between the genders of the victims, but this week the country's Human Rights Commission released figures showing that 569 women had been killed in that period (six a day on average), with another 1,052 who faced attempted murder.
Many women - already feeling unsafe - have been left reeling by recent events.
And it has put pressure on the government, less than a year after ministers acknowledged the scale of the issue and declared gender-based violence a national disaster.
Announcing the move last November, Minister of Social Development Nokuzola Sisisi Tolashe said treating the issue as a national disaster would help the government tackle the crisis.
It followed weeks of protests, culminating in a "Women's Shut Down" march as South Africa hosted the G20 summit.
This week has seen a chorus of calls for things to go further.
Rights group Amnesty International said an important first step towards protecting South Africa's women was to recognise femicide as a separate crime.

"Every day that femicide remains unrecognised as a crime is a failure to confront the targeted killing of women," said Amnesty's country director Shenilla Mohamed in a statement. "It is time to call it what it is: Femicide.
"Femicide is a gender-motivated crime. It is the killing of a woman because she is a woman."
Amnesty says femicide is criminalised as a specific crime in 33 countries, including Gabon and Morocco in Africa.
It argues that making that change in South Africa could help focus on the scale of the issue.
"It would compel the state to confront their failure to protect women and girls from violence," says Mohamed. "You cannot fix what you are not tracking."
Almost everyone in South Africa agrees more needs to be done.

President Cyril Ramaphosa this week pledged to leave "no stone unturned" in investigating the crimes in Ekurhuleni, adding: "As a nation, we must stand up for the rights, safety and dignity of women and girls."
Lebogang Ramofoko, an advocate for gender and social justice, said the levels of violence against women in the country were symptomatic of a much bigger problem – a lack of regard for humanity.

"The bodies of black women have been treated as disposable in this country for time in memorial, passed down from colonisation through to apartheid," she tells the BBC, referring to the legalised system of racism that was in place until 1994.
"What we see happening to women is testimony to legacies of violence from those systems whose traumas were never addressed.

"This is not to say black men are inherently violent, but in systems where violence was meted out against them for decades, historically black women were the people that that violence would be taken out on - that cycle has not been broken."

In Kempton Park, a district of Ekurhuleni where five of the nine recent bodies were found, Lumka Maqhubela is part of the Girl2Woman Foundation group which has held protests to raise awareness of the crimes.
"We are grieved, we are scared," she says. "If the police cannot protect us any more the government should step in and do something.

"It's clear that we are not safe, we cannot be told by the police to be more vigilant. They should be doing more to make our communities safe – what else are we expected to do? We are not safe anywhere, not in our homes, not in the streets, it needs to stop."
"I feel uncomfortable," says Thulisile Sibande, 32. "When I go to a shop, I have to look around. I'm shocked and scared. So scared, it's a trauma."
Thembi Mabena, 60, tells the BBC she lived in the same neighbourhood as Dineo Motapane.
"She was laughing every day, with everybody," she remembers. "Now I'm worried.
"I know many children, girls, who tell me they are afraid to go to the shop alone. There is no safety, even for me too. I am old, but there is no safety."
"In South Africa," says Lerato Mzizi, 20, simply, "women are not safe any more."

articles.title: A four-minute warning isn't enough: Russia's new relentless missile tactics exhaust Kyiv residents
articles.summary: Increasingly frequent and ferocious attacks on the Ukrainian capital have left many on edge.

blocks.text: A four-minute warning isn't enough: Russia's new relentless missile tactics exhaust Kyiv residents
Image source, BBC News Ukraine
Daria left her apartment in Kyiv this summer after Russia's attacks on the city intensified
ByDiana Kuryshko and Victoria Kalimbet
BBC News Ukrainian
For much of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Daria was not afraid of the shelling.

Even on nights of heavy bombardment, the 27-year-old could sleep through the explosions in her apartment in Kyiv. Like many Ukrainians, she relied on the "two-wall rule": staying safe by keeping two walls between herself and the outside world.
But this year that has changed.
In recent months, Russia has scaled up the intensity and frequency of its attacks against the Ukrainian capital.

In the first 10 days of July alone, the Russians launched dozens of ballistic missiles in three major attacks, killing nearly 60 civilians, according to official figures. Similar large scale attacks took place in August and September.
A BBC Verify analysis of government figures found Kyiv is now suffering more daily air raid alerts than at any time since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.
It was during an attack one night in May that Daria realised she no longer felt safe in her home.

She and her boyfriend were in the corridor of their ninth-floor apartment, watching a boxing match, as explosions went off around them, the blast waves causing the windows to repeatedly slam open and shut.
When the fight ended, "there was no longer anything to distract me," Daria says. "That's when I realised I was really scared."
At first, she thought she would start using a nearby bomb shelter during attacks.
But in June, when a young mother was killed running to a shelter in Kyiv, Daria decided she needed to leave the city altogether.
She returned to her family's country house, 30km (18.6 miles) away in Romankiv, and now spends a total of four hours a day commuting to and from Kyiv, where she works in the defence sector.

blocks.caption: Image caption, A photo from the State Emergency Service shows the impact of a Russian strike in July

blocks.text: Image source, Ukraine State Emergency Service
A photo from the State Emergency Service shows the impact of a Russian strike in July
Daria's experience is far from unique.

Residents in Kyiv who say they had got used to Russia's missile and drone strikes have told the BBC World Service the renewed intensity of the attacks is making them rethink how they live their lives.

Previously, Ukraine's air-defence network and military intelligence gave residents a degree of predictability. Large-scale attacks could often be detected in advance, allowing people to spend the night in shelters, leave the city or take other precautions. But since the summer, Russia has changed its tactics.

It has relied less on aircraft, whose movements can be spotted ahead of time, and more on ballistic missiles that travel at tremendous speed and provide little warning. Air-raid alerts sometimes begin only moments before impact, or even simultaneously with the first explosions.

Daria can see her nearest shelter from the window of her apartment, which she still rents. Even so, it takes around 10 minutes to reach it. During a ballistic attack, she might have just four minutes' warning or less, she says.
She decided to leave Kyiv in June after holidaying abroad this summer and seeing people living "normal" lives. Since then, she has only spent one night in Kyiv.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Ballistic missiles are difficult to detect in advance

blocks.text: Ballistic missiles are difficult to detect in advance
Yet, for many, leaving is not an option.
Sixty-two-year-old Olha Vlasova lives on the seventh floor of a high-rise apartment block with her 98-year-old mother, Nadia Tsybina.
Despite her age, Nadia remains intensely engaged with the world.
From her bed she follows events in Ukraine and abroad, discussing everything from US President Donald Trump's policies, to anti-corruption protests in Kyiv, and the Epstein files.
She's also learned that she can often tell, simply by listening, whether a Russian missile or drone has been intercepted or has reached its target.
This summer, she says she has heard fewer interceptions.
"It's upsetting when there's nothing to shoot them down with," Nadia says. "I can hear them firing with whatever they've got, rifles, machine guns."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Nadia, 98, continues to follow world events closely from her bed

blocks.text: Nadia, 98, continues to follow world events closely from her bed

blocks.caption: Image caption, Olha has taken to placing a mattress by the window to protect her and her mother from flying glass

blocks.text: Olha has taken to placing a mattress by the window to protect her and her mother from flying glass

With Nadia confined to her bed, she and Olha cannot go to a shelter, however serious an attack is. Instead, as soon as an air-raid siren sounds, Olha covers her mother with a blanket, pushes a mattress into their window frame, and then hides in a wardrobe which puts two walls between her and outside.
Nadia places a pillow over her head to protect her face from flying glass.
Once in her wardrobe, Olha will often stay awake watching the news all night.
"They come in, they bomb us," Nadia says. "You haven't even had time to fall asleep, and there's another alert. They come again, they shoot them down again. And it goes on all night.
"People don't sleep, and then they walk around like zombies."

blocks.caption: Image caption, The new academic year in Kyiv began with many students attending classes in shelters as an air raid alert was in effect in the morning

blocks.text: Image source, Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images
The new academic year in Kyiv began with many students attending classes in shelters as an air raid alert was in effect in the morning
An increase in daytime attacks means life in Kyiv is now interrupted by air raid sirens day and night.
At the beginning of September, when children returned to school after the summer break, there were dozens of air raid alerts, followed by explosions and fires.
According to Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko, two children were injured in attacks on 31 August.
As a result, many children stayed at home, while others spent hours in the basements of schools and kindergartens.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Commuters in Kyiv have become accustomed to long wait times as the metro is disrupted.

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Commuters in Kyiv have become accustomed to long wait times as the metro is disrupted.

When the sirens sound, it also affects businesses and transport. Shopping centres close and above-ground metro stations suspend operations, often severing public transport links between Kyiv's Left and Right Banks, on either side of the Dnieper River, for hours at a time.
New metro operating rules during air raid alerts are being introduced in an attempt to improve the situation.
For Olha, it has meant seeing less of her eight-year-old granddaughter, who lives on the other side of the city.

She knows if her granddaughter comes to visit, she risks struggling to return home. When metro services stop running, expensive cab journeys are Olha's only option. Crossing the river can cost as much as 1,000 hryvnias ($22, £16.6), she says, just under one-eighth of Ukraine's monthly minimum wage.
The experience has left her frustrated with what she sees as hesitation by some of Ukraine's foreign partners to provide additional air-defence missiles.
President Volodymyr Zelensky has repeatedly appealed to allies for additional air-defence systems and interceptor missiles.

"They [Ukraine's allies] wait, thinking: 'What if we get attacked?'" Olha says. "It's like refusing to give medicine to a cancer patient because you're saying, 'What if I get sick one day?' Well, maybe you won't. Give it away before it expires."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Neither Natalia nor her daughter can sleep through the nightly attacks

blocks.text: Image source, Natalia Bushkovska
Neither Natalia nor her daughter can sleep through the nightly attacks
In another part of the city, mother-of-two Natalia Bushkovska each night rehearses three different plans.
Plan A is to spread bedding in the hallway behind two interior walls; Plan B is to move the family into the building's shared corridor; and Plan C is to head for the basement.
Even there, she admits, she does not feel entirely safe.
"I keep a backpack with essential items," says Natalia, 37. "There's a tourniquet for severe bleeding. I also keep a whistle, just in case.
"If the worst happens, rescuers will be able to find us under the rubble."
Her nine-year-old daughter has her own emergency bag containing toys, lip balm and a tourniquet. Like her 12-year-old brother, she learned how to use a tourniquet through first-aid training.
Natalia says the constant attacks are exhausting.
While her son often sleeps through them, she and her daughter wake up almost every time.
"Because of the attacks, I don't get enough sleep," she says. "Now, in the fifth year of the war, I find it increasingly difficult to bounce back after nights like these."
The growing intensity of the strikes, she says, is taking a psychological toll across the city.
"People are exhausted. They don't have enough time to recover."

On Thursday 17 September, Russia launched a ballistic missile attack on Kyiv. According to Mayor Vitali Klitschko, 20 people were injured in the attack. Among the wounded were two children, aged 10 and 12.
Additional reporting by Janet Ball
More weekend picks

articles.title: US and Denmark reach security deal after Trump’s threats to take island
articles.summary:
The agreement would allow the US to expand its military presence, while Denmark and Greenland say it preserves their sovereignty and right to self-determination

Donald Trump announced on…

blocks.text: Donald Trump announced on Friday that the US had struck an Arctic security pact with the leaders of Denmark and Greenland, after threatening for months to take Greenland by force.

The US president cast the deal as a personal triumph, claiming in a post on Truth Social that the “very important, historic, and special” agreement “gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland, completely addressing ALL of our many U.S. concerns”.

“We will immediately begin the process of developing a large Military presence in the appropriate part of Greenland,” Trump added. The US already has a presence on the island, and the right to expand bases, through Nato.
Greenland is a self-governing territory of the Kingdom of Denmark, a fellow Nato member.

In his post, Trump said that the agreement means “no US adversary can EVER have a base in Greenland, have a military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval”.
The US and Denmark will formally sign the agreement next week, on the sidelines of the United Nations general assembly in New York City, according to the Danish government.

Statements from Denmark’s prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, and the leader of Greenland’s government, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, posted online late Friday, emphasized that the agreement would fall far short of Trump’s stated desire for “the acquisition of Greenland by the United States”.
Frederiksen said that the agreement “recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination”.

Nielsen said the agreement “ensures and strengthens the security of Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark, the United States and the Western alliance”, suggesting that the deal might possibly just reiterate the existing US rights through Nato to use the island as a security base.
Once agreed to, the pact will need to go through parliamentary procedures to be enacted, the statement said.

At a Nato summit in Ankara earlier this year, Trump renewed his bid for the US to acquire Greenland, threatening to pull all American armed forces out of Europe after the continent repeatedly pushed back.

articles.title: US and Denmark reach deal over Greenland's security
articles.summary: Trump said the agreement will give the US "permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland", though specifics haven't been confirmed by Danish officials.

blocks.text: The US and Denmark have announced a deal on Greenland's security and say the agreement will be signed next week.
US President Donald Trump said the agreement would grant the US "permanent control over security, and all other needs".
Denmark's Prime Minister said the deal "strengthens security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic area" but did not address specifics in the agreement that Trump mentioned in a social media post.
The deal comes after months of threats by Trump to "take" Greenland over national security concerns, citing its strategic location for defence purposes and its mineral wealth.

Trump, in a post on Truth Social, said the deal comes with "no cost to the United States" and will grant the US the ability to "to do what is necessary" to "secure and defend the security of Greenland".
He said the deal includes a rule that no US adversary can maintain a military presence in Greenland or "make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval".
Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen confirmed that the agreement will be signed at the United Nations General Assembly next week.

She said the agreement "strengthens our common security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic area" while also "at the same time recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination".
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio called it a "historic deal" and a "huge win for the United States and the American people".
"This deal permanently and completely addresses our national security concerns in Greenland," he told Fox News.

articles.title: Greenland, Denmark say deal with U.S. will not cede sovereignty

image.caption: Kenneth A. Howery, the U.S. ambassador to Denmark, is shown with Vivian Motzfeldt, right, a member of Greenland's parliament, at the opening of a new U.S. Consulate in Nuuk, Greenland, on May 21. (Tim Barsoe/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

Denmark and Greenland on Saturday said any agreement with the United States would not compromise Greenland's sovereignty, after President Donald Trump said the deal would give Washington "permanent control" over the Arctic island's security, leaving its precise scope unclear.
Agreement follows months of tension over Trump's threats to seize Greenland

Denmark and Greenland on Saturday said any agreement with the United States would not compromise Greenland's sovereignty, after U.S. President Donald Trump said the deal would give Washington "permanent control" over the Arctic island's security, leaving its precise scope unclear.

The U.S., Denmark and Greenland said late on Friday they had entered into an agreement for the U.S. to ‌develop a significant military presence on Greenland, while prohibiting American adversaries from building their own bases on the island.

Key details of the agreement have not been made public, including the degree of U.S. military presence in the self-governed ⁠Danish territory and whether any formal power over foreign policy and resources would be ceded to Washington.

Denmark and Greenland expressed hope that a deal, which is expected to be signed during the United Nations General Assembly next week, would end months of uncertainty triggered by Trump's threats to seize control of Greenland. Parliamentary action is still needed by the governments of Denmark and Greenland before it can be enforced.
"Next week could be a good week — for Greenland, Denmark, and the United States," Danish Foreign Affairs Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen said in a statement posted on Facebook on Saturday.

items: Trump says deal struck to boost U.S. military presence in Greenland

blocks.text: "A time of uncertainty will hopefully give way to a binding agreement that strengthens security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic, and thereby our shared security within NATO and Europe — while respecting the [Danish] Kingdom's red lines," Rasmussen said.
Denmark and Greenland have repeatedly insisted that Washington respect the sovereignty of the Danish kingdom and accept that Greenland is not for sale.

Trump said on his Truth Social platform late on Friday that under a deal, "the United States will FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the security of Greenland, and the United States of America."

The deal "gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland," he said, adding that no adversary would ever be permitted to have a base or military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments there, without Washington's express written approval.
Deal struck to boost U.S. military presence in Greenland: Trump
NATO welcomes agreement
Trump made the announcement after Reuters exclusively reported that the U.S. and Denmark were closing in on a deal.

"This is probably not the end of President Trump’s ambitions for Greenland and certainly not the end of U.S. strategic interest in the territory and its resources," said Mikkel Vedby Rasmussen, a political science professor at the University of Copenhagen, in Denmark's capital.

If the Danish government cedes any formal power to Washington, it raises the question in Greenland of whether "this is the beginning of replacing the colonial relationship with Denmark with a colonial relationship to the United States," he said.

"I am pleased on Greenland's behalf that we are nearing the conclusion of an agreement — an agreement that benefits not only our collective security but also the continued development of this country," Jens-Frederik Nielsen, Greenland's prime minister, said on Saturday in a post on Facebook.
"The agreement recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of our Kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination."
Does Iceland feel threatened by Trump's expansionist threats? | Hanomansing Tonight

Trump's threats, which peaked in January, triggered a diplomatic crisis that strained relations within the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and pushed Denmark and Greenland into negotiations aimed at defusing the pressure.
A NATO spokesperson on Saturday said the alliance welcomed the agreement, which would "help advance security, stability and co-operation in this vital region."
Steffen Nielsen, a 49-year-old sales worker living in Copenhagen, told Reuters: "I think that the U.S. is probably going to get what they could have had the whole time, if they just asked nicely."

"I don't like it," Kaj Jorgensen, an 80-year-old pensioner, also living in Copenhagen, said of the news. "I don't wish the United States to be present anywhere in the Danish Kingdom. I really don't trust Donald Trump."

articles.title: Blumentritt descendants donate rare Rizal letter, other 19th-century items to National Museum
articles.summary: VIENNA, Austria - The National Museum of the Philippines has acquired three sets of 19th-century heirlooms kept by descendants of Austro-Hungarian ethnographer Ferdinand Blumentritt.

blocks.text: VIENNA, Austria - The National Museum of the Philippines has acquired three sets of 19th-century heirlooms kept by descendants of Austro-Hungarian ethnographer Ferdinand Blumentritt.

The items, long in the possession of Blumentritt’s great-great-granddaughter Elke Pickert, include an unpublished letter from Jose Rizal, a pair of watercolor paintings by Juan Luna, and a 19th-century Japanese parasol with an embroidered earlier version of the Philippine flag.
For over a century, these historical treasures remained tucked away in Kufstein, Austria, the ancestral home of Pickert’s grandmother, Dolores Blumentritt.

“The precious objects have been a part of our family history for many decades,” Pickert shared in a ceremonial turnover ceremony attended by officials from the National Museum of the Philippines and the Philippine Embassy in Vienna, as well as diplomats, academics, and local community members on Thursday.
Pickert told GMA News about her joy of having these items showcased in the Philippines. “I’m proud that it’s going to the Philippines, to the National Museum, and a lot of people can see it.”
Treasure trove
The heirlooms were discovered by Austrian anthropologist Dr. Johann Stockinger in 2017, upon visiting Pickert’s home in Kufstein for his previous research on Blumentritt.
Although Stockinger knew about Pickert’s lineage, he was unaware that the family had kept the historical items safe, including the portraits of Dolores.
“I saw the portraits hanging on the wall. I asked Elke, ‘Do you know who painted these?’ She said, ‘No’”, Stockinger told GMA News.

Stockinger quickly identified the artwork as original watercolor portraits of 25-year-old Dolores painted by Juan Luna in Leitmeritz (present-day Litomerice in the Czech Republic) in April 1899, signed “Recuerdos de LVNA”. The other portrait bore the sign, “LVNA 99”.
“I had to explain their significance to her. I was then allowed to rummage through a few boxes of old documents. In the process, I discovered Rizal’s letter to Blumentritt dated May 9, 1894.”

Stockinger was referring to the unpublished three-page letter Rizal wrote from his exile in Dapitan in May 1896. Here, the hero sent his greetings to Blumentritt and his daughter Dolores, whom he called “Loleng”.
The anthropologist also recalled a detail from Blumentritt’s old correspondence to German anthropologist Adolf Benhard Meyer about a wedding present sent from Kobe, Japan.

“I read in Blumentritt’s letter to A. B. Meyer dated April 29, 1900: ‘Loleng’s wedding will take place on May 17. She received a silk umbrella with the flag of the Philippine Republic embroidered on it from a Filipino living in Kobe.’ I then asked Elke if they still had this umbrella, and sure enough, she was able to find it in the basement.”
“She went down to her cellar, and she found it, after more than a century,” Stockinger said.

blocks.caption: During the turnover ceremony on September 17, 2026, National Museum Deputy Director-General for Museums Arvin Manuel Villalon offered a deeper insight into the artifacts and their contemporary relevance. Photo: Andy Peñafuerte III

blocks.text: During the turnover ceremony on September 17, 2026, National Museum Deputy Director-General for Museums Arvin Manuel Villalon offered a deeper insight into the artifacts and their contemporary relevance. Photo: Andy Peñafuerte III
A glimpse into Philippine-Austrian friendship

Rizal’s unpublished letter from Dapitan, written in Spanish and German and addressed to Blumentritt, describes his activities while in exile, including sending a collection of butterflies to Europe and treating indigenous patients.

The correspondence also reveals Rizal’s playful relationship with Loleng, which National Museum Deputy Director-General for Museums Arvin Manuel Villalon believes may have helped preserve the document through generations.

blocks.caption: This letter was written by Jose Rizal in Spanish and sent to Dr. Ferdinand Blumentritt on May 9, 1894. It was a letter greeting Blumentritt's daughter, Dolores, whom Rizal called Loleng. Photo: Andy Peñafuerte III.

blocks.text: This letter was written by Jose Rizal in Spanish and sent to Dr. Ferdinand Blumentritt on May 9, 1894. It was a letter greeting Blumentritt's daughter, Dolores, whom Rizal called Loleng. Photo: Andy Peñafuerte III

Teasing Loleng’s disinterest in mathematics, Rizal wrote: “Why learn quadratic equations and root extraction if you ultimately won’t have enough time to take care of your home and your children? I prefer that they learn about hygiene, hygiene, and hygiene. And later, a little bit more of domestic medicine, especially children's and women's diseases.”

Rizal closed his letter: “My mother and sister send their regards, especially to Frau Blumentritt and Loleng”, before sharing a German quote: “Tausend Grüße von Haus zu Haus, über Land und Meer” (A thousand greetings from house to house, across land and sea).

For the portraits, Luna and Felipe Agoncillo–serving then as diplomats of the First Philippine Republic–visited the Blumentritt family in Leitmeritz between April and May 1899. During this period, Luna painted several artworks, including portraits of Blumentritt and his daughter.

blocks.caption: These watercolor portraits of Loleng Blumentritt were painted by Juan Luna when he visited Leitmeritz (present-day Litomerice in the Czech Republic) in April 1899. Photo: Andy Peñafuerte III

blocks.text: These watercolor portraits of Loleng Blumentritt were painted by Juan Luna when he visited Leitmeritz (present-day Litomerice in the Czech Republic) in April 1899. Photo: Andy Peñafuerte III

Loleng’s watercolor portraits show the fashion at the time: she wears puffy sleeves known as gigot and what looks like a Victorian velvet choker. Her hair is neatly arranged in a high chignon, with soft curls in the front.

“All in all, she was likely quite fashionable as befits the daughter of a prominent gentleman scholar. And we regard these portraits as small artistic treasures that tell us so much of this important circle of relationships,” Villalon said.
The third item is a traditional Japanese silk umbrella embroidered with wisteria, chrysanthemums, and a hoisted Philippine flag.
It was sent from Japan by diplomat Mariano Ponce as a wedding gift to Dolores, who would marry Karl Pickert in 1900.

Ponce, chosen by Emilio Aguinaldo to represent the Philippine Republic, procured the umbrella made of white silk called habutai. It was embroidered with chrysanthemum, wisteria, butterfly motifs, and an embroidery of a Philippine flag hoisted on a bamboo pole.

blocks.caption: This Japanese parasol, made of white silk and decorated with embroidery of chrysanthemum, wisteria, and the then-Philippine flag, was a wedding gift from the Aguinaldo government to Loleng Blumentritt and Karl Pickert. Photo: Andy Peñafuerte III

blocks.text: This Japanese parasol, made of white silk and decorated with embroidery of chrysanthemum, wisteria, and the then-Philippine flag, was a wedding gift from the Aguinaldo government to Loleng Blumentritt and Karl Pickert. Photo: Andy Peñafuerte III
The gesture was part of a larger tribute where Aguinaldo’s revolutionary government covered Dolores's entire wedding expenses, according to Villalon.

“The letter, the portraits, and the umbrella also show the endearing qualities of Filipino values, such as utang na loob or reciprocity, familial ties, and, of course, cherished friendships, the friendship between the Blumentritts and, of course, our hero, Dr. Jose Rizal,” Villalon added.
Older than the Philippines and Austria
Some of these historical objects are older than the republics of the Philippines and Austria, Philippine Ambassador to Austria Evangelina Lourdes Bernas noted.
So, most Filipino and Austrian guests at the turnover ceremony stood in awe to see these heirlooms in person.
Bernas said that the objects stand as “a testament to the ties of friendship between our countries that are much older than our formal bilateral diplomatic relations”.
National Museum Director-General Jeremy Barns described the acquisition as “super nakakataba ng puso (heartwarming)”, stressing how it shows family connections and friendships.

“It’s like a window into the time of Rizal and his friendship with Blumentritt. Here’s another opportunity to dive a bit deeper and ask, ‘Who is Blumentritt and what is his importance? What is his relationship with Jose Rizal?’ We’re enriched by stories like this, and these objects prove that these stories really happened,” Barns told GMA News.
National Museum Board of Trustees Chairman Andoni Aboitiz added that the items symbolize the Philippines today: “an international, cosmopolitan, and very reflective people”.

“My wish is that the people realize that this is a symbol of who we are today, not just of what happened in the past, but who we are today: open, free, and people who are always looking for new ideas and not resistant to change," he said.
For anthropologist Dr. Hermann Muckler from the Austro-Philippine Society, the pieces symbolize “a very close and very relaxed and even very productive relationship”.

“This brings us here in Austria closer to the Philippines. And thanks to Johan Stockinger, who was for a long time the president of the Austro-Philippine Society. He is still on the board, in a very important function where he is digging into the history of this personal relationship between Rizal and Blumentritt. So, it’s quite likely that new findings will surface in the near future," Muckler said.
According to Barns, the items are set to be presented in an upgraded gallery at the National Museum in Manila next year. —VBL, GMA News

articles.title: The 9 best of a TIFF grappling with a world coming apart
articles.summary: Like every year, the Toronto International Film Festival’s 51st iteration boasted a basket of incredible, now-buzzy titles for the coming year. This year, many were about people — overwhelmingly…

image.caption: Jordan Firstman's first-time feature Club Kid feels anything but amateurish. (A24)

blocks.text: Entertainment

Like every year, the Toronto International Film Festival’s 51st iteration boasted a basket of incredible, now-buzzy titles for the coming year. This year, many were about people — overwhelmingly young people — grappling with a confusing and fracturing world and the feeling they weren't made for it.
The Debut, Club Kid and more land as decisive triumphs at the Toronto International Film Festival
Like every year, the Toronto International Film Festival's 51st iteration boasted a basket of incredible, now-buzzy titles for the coming year.

And like most years, the best of those films seemed to fit a theme. This year, it was characters in a sort of psychic crisis: people — overwhelmingly young people — grappling with a confusing and fracturing world and the feeling they weren't made for it.
To navigate those stories of crying and comedy, we've put together a list of some of the best.
The Debut
A kaleidoscopic carnival of comedy and grotesquerie. An unpleasant and fascinating story of self-improvement and self-immolation. Taxi Driver for theatre kids.

In short, Jesse Eisenberg's The Debut is a sure-to-be-divisive, sure-to-entertain work of art. Showcasing Julianne Moore as a terrifyingly terrible community theatre actress and Paul Giamatti as her Whiplash meets Dead Poets Society mentor, its offbeat narrative style is paired with Moore's transformative performance of a lifetime. You might love it. You might hate it. But either way, you shouldn't miss it.
Club Kid

Writer/director/star Jordan Firstman's first-time feature feels anything but amateurish. The familiar story it tells, that of a disaffected young man (Peter) suddenly tasked with taking care of a son (Arlo) he never knew he had, would be enough for a good movie. But as soon as the sentimental comedy/drama steamrolls through the normal "reluctant mentor" story beats, it flips and crashes into something more.
The result is a star turn for just about everyone you see on screen (including Peter's odd roommate Nicky, played by Debut supporting actor Eldar Isgandarov). It also just might make you cry.

items: The Debut is totally going to win an Oscar
Club Kid is one of TIFF's best. It might make you cry

blocks.text: Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother

Bassam Tariq's singular vision — both in terms of the movie's religious themes and gorgeously stylized cinematography — makes Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother something special. On top of that, star Mahershala Ali as Latif and his co-stars make it something incredible.

But it is Latif himself, a reluctant hitman who's lost his wife, nearly lost his faith, and is soon sent on a whirlwind mission to help a lost rich brat survive the week, that propels the story forward. It's a near-indefinable collage of styles and genres — birthdays, broken glass, smiles and tears — but one that is nearly impossible to look away from.
Julián

As he's dropped off at his grandma's house in Brooklyn for the summer, the star of hand-drawn Canadian co-production Julián (Knyght Darius Jack) is already off-balance. But a niggling sense of unease sets everything on edge: there is something pushing back against the person whom Julián wants to be, how he wants to act and what he's allowed to care about. That confusing, bigger-than-him battle pitches into a higher gear when he tries to join the local girls in making glamorous mermaid costumes for an upcoming parade.
For some reason he can't fathom, the world keeps telling him the person he wants to be is wrong. And as the movie proceeds to show, the world is better when we fix that.
Iron Boy

From Pixar animator Louis Clichy (and starring his own son, Gary, in the lead role) Iron Boy is another animated tale of fitting in. A French farm boy with a pernicious case of scoliosis, Christophe, 10, can't seem to keep things straight. He's fighting with his overbearing father, getting into trouble at school — and literally falling over at every opportunity. Our young hero is soon fitted with an iron back brace to keep things from tumbling into chaos.

Unsurprisingly, things don't go exactly to plan. Iron Boy's resultant charting of failure to meet expectations, first loves and redemptive self-acceptance is as much grounded character study as it is magical realism. Its entirely hand-drawn animation style is also a rare and beautiful sight to behold.
Toy Gun Bandit
Like if the infamously over-the-top "Montana Meth Project" anti-drug ads from the early 2000s had made a feature film, Toy Gun Bandit says "not even once" to robbing your local gas station.

Unfortunately, our star apparently never saw those ads. Instead, French-Canadian teen Félix makes bad choice after bad choice, sending his legal situation spiralling from bad to astronomically worse in a cautionary tale that reads like a modern day Reefer Madness.

What keeps the eclectic, almost incidental plot from fraying into nothingness is Felix himself: first-time actor Félix Munger — a true revelation — plays the desperate-for-attention eponymous protagonist with an electric, vulnerable and mesmerizing charisma. The film pairs wonderfully with TIFF's other Canadian teen-on-the-run film, In Alaska, as both are character studies grounded by powerhouse young performances. With Munger in front of the camera of Toy Gun Bandit, you cannot help but root — and mourn — for the bright future he constructs, then inevitably destroys.
Sunburn

Like street photography in motion, Sunburn makes the everyday fascinating — with serious thanks owed to François Truffaut's Small Change. The plot is as subtle as it is personal: a group of young people try to make sense of themselves, and each other, in Toronto's St. James Town neighbourhood during a heat wave.

And like TIFF's other teen-ensemble triumph La Gradiva, the true story is under the surface — though in Sunburn, that truth isn't quite so heart-rendingly tragic. What lifts Serville Poblete's coming-of-age hodgepodge to the next level despite its conversely light tone is the serious talent he displays for capturing and evoking senses and sensations.

The visceral capturing of dripping ice cream on a sweltering day. Of open mouths and dripping sweat. Of bursting pimples and bursting waterballoons and the general exuberance of real life. Every joyfully real aspect of the world he clearly knows so well is delivered in a dreamlike package.
Eklipse

"What did I do to you?" asks Tomy of his friend Chris — or the boy who used to be his friend. As Eklipse drifts from Tree of Life-esque shots of the trees, cattle and mountains of its Tyrolean Alps setting, the two drift further and further apart. And Tomy has no idea why.

However, we know it is because Tomy's father has contracted AIDS, a terrifying and misunderstood death sentence in this rural and remote 1990s setting — though no one has told Tomy. The tender and withholding, riddle-like feature from Manuel Wetscher is the kind many will hate: "Nothing even happens" will likely be a common critique.
But if you like solving a riddle, there's a wealth of painful, twist-the-knife messages just waiting to break your heart.
The Smell of Apples

Speaking of heartbreaking, that's something The Smell of Apples can deliver in spades. A view of apartheid South Africa told from the perspective of a white child reckoning with the sins of his father, you could call it Zone of Interest refracted through a psychically destructive coming-of-age story.

Or you could call it a serious Academy Award best international film contender, one made with such power and aplomb it would be an indictment to ignore. Or you could just call it what it is: incredible.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jackson Weaver is a reporter and film critic for CBC's entertainment news team in Toronto. You can reach him at jackson.weaver@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Trump signs sweeping Russia sanctions bill
articles.summary: The bill is named after the late Senator Lindsey Graham, a staunch advocate of aid for Ukraine.

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump has signed a sweeping sanctions bill, taking aim at Russia's economy by punishing major purchasers of its oil and gas.

The bill, passed by the US House of Representatives earlier this week, gives Trump broad powers to levy tariffs of up to 100% on the top five purchasers of Russian oil and gas – most significantly China and India.
At Trump's behest, the bill also extends to Iran's energy and weapons sectors.
The bill is named after the late Senator Lindsey Graham, one of Ukraine's staunchest defenders in Washington before his death on 11 July.

The 48-page bill, formally titled the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, includes exceptions for countries that import less than 15% of their natural gas from Russia and are working to lessen their dependency.

Additionally, the bill includes sanctions against Russian President Vladimir Putin, senior figures within the Russian government as well as banks and other financial institutions and Russia's "shadow fleet" of tankers used to circumvent existing sanctions.
Senator Richard Blumenthal, a New York Democrat, previously described the legislation as "scorching sanctions" which would "throttle Putin's war machine".
Data from the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air, or CREA, shows that China accounted for 50% of Russian crude exports between December 2022 and August 2026, followed by India at 37%.
Turkey and the European Union each accounted for 5% during the same time period, although Russian energy exports to the EU have been decreasing.
Senator Graham had long sought to push the Trump administration to do more to punish Russia for the war that followed its invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
The bill also had the support of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who praised its passage by the House of Representatives earlier this week.

"It is symbolic that the US House of Representatives' passage of Lindsey Graham's sanctions bill took place on the night of yet another Russian attack on Ukraine involving ballistic missiles, other missiles, and drones," Zelensky wrote on Telegram on 17 September.
Graham, 71, died on 11 July of an "aortic dissection" caused by cardiovascular disease shortly after returning from a trip to Kyiv.
"He died doing the work he was born to do," Trump said at the time.

Prior to his death, he was widely considered one of Ukraine's fiercest allies on Capitol Hill, at a time when Republicans were bitterly divided over the extent of US involvement abroad and the amount of aid being given to Ukraine.

articles.title: Men deported from US bound and beaten in Equatorial Guinea detention hotel, lawyers say
articles.summary:
Group trapped at Hotel Bamy after US removal as rights groups sound alarm over poor conditions and violence

Two men that the Trump administration expelled to Equatorial Guinea were…

blocks.text: Two men that the Trump administration expelled to Equatorial Guinea were bound, fitted with bags over their heads, beaten and pushed down a flight of stairs, all in plain view of other US deportees, according to witnesses and human rights lawyers.

The men – one from Egypt and one from Eritrea – were then taken to a prison. About 30 detainees from the US remain trapped at a hotel in the outskirts of the coastal city of Malabo after being deported from the US. Detainees have said they believe the men were beaten for telling the press and human rights advocates about the poor conditions and violence inside the hotel, and that they are haunted by flashbacks and terrified they will be retaliated against next.
Human rights advocates and experts have warned for months that conditions at the Hotel Bamy – a run-down establishment that has served as a detention center for US deportees – are dangerous.

The US has sent at least 66 people from different African countries, Cuba and Brazil to Equatorial Guinea, which has received $7.5m as part of a deal to cooperate with the US deportation program. The Trump administration has pursued dozens of similar deals with countries to take in immigrants that the US cannot deport directly to their home countries, where judges have deemed they would face torture or persecution. In the past, the US government allowed those people to live and work in the US indefinitely.
The Trump administration, however, has sought instead to expel them to third countries where they have no ties, do not speak the local language and have no legal status – trapping them in limbo.

Advocates have been especially concerned for deportees sent to Equatorial Guinea, where the authoritarian government is notorious for human rights abuses, including torture, according to the US state department. Detainees held at Hotel Bamy have told the Guardian that armed guards keep watch over them 24/7, and that they have not been provided any medical care or even fresh clothes since arriving there. One of the detainees, who has a severe stomach hernia that requires visits to the hospital to drain his stomach due excessive fluid build-up, said he has been unable to see a doctor since arriving at Hotel Bamy.
Other detainees have managed to obtain medication for HIV, diabetes and other conditions via human rights lawyers, but remain fearful that access to medications will be arbitrarily cut off.

The two men who were tortured – Ahmed Soliman, 31, of Egypt, and Samson Birhane, 47, of Eritrea – have since been transferred to a prison in Malabo. Multiple witnesses recounted that the police officers shouted, “Where is the phone? Where is the phone!” as they beat the men, who had initially been accused of breaking a mirror at the hotel before they were pulled aside and arrested.

The beating, which occurred on 11 September, followed the release of a video first reported by Reuters showing conditions at the hotel and the violent behavior of the guards. The detainees had been using cellphones to communicate with lawyers and the media about the conditions they were facing.

blocks.caption: Equatorial Guinea police point gun at migrants deported by Trump administration - loop

blocks.text: In the video taken by Soliman, which lawyers shared with the Guardian, authorities are seen pointing guns at the deportees. A Cuban man asked the officer for the return of his confiscated mobile phone ​so he could contact relatives and a ​lawyer, but was ignored. When officers noticed Soliman filming the exchange with his mobile phone, multiple officers rushed at him and others standing nearby, pointed their guns, and told Soliman to remain on his knees with his hands up for 10-15 minutes.

In another video, Soliman was able to film authorities forcibly sending US deportees to Ethiopia, where they are likely to face torture. When deportees resisted going with authorities, officials gave them the option to “go back to their home country” or “go to prison”. At least 12 people have been returned by Equatorial Guinea to their home country, where they face persecution.

In May, human rights experts at the United Nations issued a rare public appeal asking Equatorial Guinea to halt plans to return deportees to their home countries and to comply with international human rights standards and avoid refoulement, or the expulsion of people to countries where they face persecution.

“This is a human rights catastrophe,” said Bella Mosselmans, director of the Global Strategic Litigation Council, who represents several of the deportees at Hotel Bamy. The US and Equatorial Guinea “must be held accountable for the atrocities they are committing”, she added.

In the week since Soliman and Birhane were beaten, police have also been searching the other detainees’ hotel rooms for cellphones, and have confiscated them. They have also barred lawyers from seeing the deportees. Authorities have told the 29 US deportees who remain at Hotel Bamy that they may never see Soliman or Birhane again, according to lawyers. One detainee who witnessed the beating said authorities treat them as if they are “blanks” who “don’t even exist”. Another detainee said an officer told her: “You will disappear from the earth. I am the law.”
Witnesses said they feared for the lives of Soliman and Birhane, who came to the US as children.

Soliman is a gay man from Egypt who had lived in Phoenix for most of his life. He had a green card, but lost status after he was convicted of drug possession. He served time for his crimes, and in October, a judge had determined he would face persecution and torture if he were to return to Egypt due to his sexuality.

Birhane had come to the US as a refugee when he was 13, but lost status after a conviction for robbery when he was in high school, in 1988. He was allowed to remain in the US after a judge ruled he faced torture in Eritrea, and had been regularly checking in with Immigration and Customs Enforcement as required.

Lawyers for the deportees shared copies of multiple emails they had sent to the US embassy in Equatorial Guinea alerting them to threats and violence against those detained at Hotel Bamy, but those messages have gone unanswered, they said. In July, amid a lawsuit challenging conditions for deportees, the African Commission issued an urgent interim order instructing the government of Equatorial Guinea to refrain from deporting, transferring, or relocating deportees against their will.
The US Department of Homeland Security did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment.
A spokesperson for the state department said: “The US government will use all legal means to remove those with no right to remain in our country.”
The agency did not respond to questions about whether it was aware of how Equatorial Guinea was treating US deportees, nor would it acknowledge whether any measures have been taken to intervene.
“As a general matter, we do not comment on the details of our private diplomatic communications with other governments,” the spokesperson said.

articles.title: UP students stage walkout over 2027 budget cuts, Pax Silica
articles.summary: Around 6,000 students, teachers, and officials from the University of the Philippines Los Baños (UPLB) joined a walkout on Friday to protest issues including education budget cuts and the proposed…

blocks.text: Published September 19, 2026 5:20am

Around 6,000 students, teachers, and officials from the University of the Philippines Los Baños (UPLB) joined a walkout on Friday to protest issues including education budget cuts and the proposed Pax Silica initiative.

In a video posted online by UPLB Perspective, students from various UPLB departments were seen joining the protest and chanting calls for accountability over corruption and the defense of people’s rights.
In a statement, the UPLB Student Council said the walkout drew thousands of participants despite heavy rainfall.
The student body reiterated its call to hold accountable those behind billions of pesos in anomalous flood control projects.

“Kung matatandaan natin, noong nakaraang taon ay 7,000 na indibidwal ang nakiisa sa walkout na ginanap hinggil sa bilyon-bilyong pisong halagang pondo na ninakaw mula sa mga mamamayan para sa mga ghost flood control projects,” the UPLB Student Council said.
(If we recall, 7,000 individuals participated in last year’s walkout over the billions of pesos in public funds stolen from the people for ghost flood control projects.)

“Ngunit magpahanggang ngayon ay hindi pa rin nakukulong ang lahat ng mga sangkot, at patuloy pa rin na nagpapakasasa sa pera ng mamamayang ninakawan nila ang mga korakot habang ang sambayanang Pilipino ay patuloy pa rin na lumulusong sa baha, nawawalan ng tahanan, naaantala ang kabuhayan, at nasasawi ang mga buhay,” it added.

(Yet up to now, not all those involved have been jailed, and corrupt officials continue to feast on the people’s stolen money while Filipinos continue to wade through floods, lose their homes, suffer disruptions to their livelihoods, and lose their lives.)
Students from the University of the Philippines Diliman (UPD) likewise staged a demonstration, raising similar concerns.
The UPD Student Council said around 3,000 students joined the walkout.
In a statement, the UPD student body cited reports of farmers and Indigenous Peoples in Tarlac being displaced to clear land for the proposed Pax Silica project.
“Huwad ang development na ito dahil alam nating lahat na ang proyektong ito ay para lamang sa gahamang interes ng mga nasa tuktok,” it said.
(This development is a lie because we all know that this project is solely for the greedy interests of those at the top.)
The UPD Student Council also cited a potential P2.95 billion reduction in funding for the UP System under the proposed 2027 national budget.
UPLB and UPD are set to hold protests on September 21, marking the 54th anniversary of the declaration of martial law under former President Ferdinand Marcos Sr. —VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Doctors say B.C. Supreme Court ruling on foreign-trained doctors a 'blow' for rural health care
articles.summary: Local doctors are speaking out after the Supreme Court ruled the B.C. government can’t force foreign-trained doctors to work in rural and remote areas.

image.caption: A B.C. Supreme Court judge recently ruled foreign-trained doctors cannot be required to practise in rural or remote locations. (Andrew Kurjata/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia
Local doctors are speaking out after the Supreme Court ruled the B.C. government can’t force foreign-trained doctors to work in rural and remote areas.
Court ruled physicians trained outside of Canada can't be required to work in remote areas
Doctors are speaking out after the B.C. Supreme Court ruled the province can’t force foreign-trained doctors to work in "underserviced" areas
“It’s another nail in the coffin of rural healthcare,” said Charles Helm, a semi-retired physician who has worked in Tumbler Ridge — a small community in B.C.’s Peace Region — for more than 30 years.
Currently, doctors trained in non-Canadian schools are required to live and practise in rural or remote locations in the province for two or three years.
Justice Matthew Kirchner ruled last week the government is not authorized to impose this requirement.
B.C. Health Minister Ravi Kahlon said legal teams are reviewing the decision and the ministry will do "whatever is required to make sure the program continues to function."

items: Hospital ER in 100 Mile House, B.C., closes temporarily for 2nd time in 2026

blocks.text: Helm said it was one of the few programs that provided an advantage for rural communities, many of which he says are in desperate need of doctors.
“We see the ongoing erosion of our health care and this ruling is just going to be another in a series of events which make it harder for us to try and recruit and retain physicians.”
Helm said three years ago, his community had four doctors, one of whom came through the foreign-trained doctor program.
Today, only one remains.
“This is absolutely catastrophic,” said Helm. “It’s another blow for rural health care.”
Can virtual care services solve the health-care staffing crisis in rural B.C.?

Paul Adams, the executive director of the B.C. Rural Health Network, said last week’s ruling will have a significant impact on remote communities across the province — many of which are reliant on the program to fill positions.
“It is an essential program,” he said.
“We can’t keep pushing people further to the edge, we need to actually reach those people as a priority.”
Alternative solutions
In the short term, Helm said incentives should be offered to doctors who move to and work in rural and remote areas.
Helm said working in rural healthcare is fulfilling, adding that the province needs to highlight this to potential incoming doctors as part of a long-term solution.
“To me, rural healthcare is what it’s all about,” he said.
“It’s the most rewarding ... and I’ve never understood why we don’t have a long lineup of doctors wanting to work here.”

items: Rural emergency room closures put pressure on B.C. paramedics: union

blocks.text: Adams said there is no one-stop shop solution to the lack of health care in remote communities, but certain steps can be taken.
He said the government could focus on expanding health-care teams in rural communities, including utilizing nurse practitioners.
“There’s a lot of work to do,” said Adams. “I think we need to think outside of the current box.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Michelle Gomez is a writer and reporter at CBC Vancouver. You can contact her at michelle.gomez@cbc.ca.
